title: Ravens Week 10 Rookie Report: Vega Ioane Leaves Early With Injury, Ja'Kobi Lane Misses Key Opportunities
full_text:
Several members of the Baltimore Ravens' 2026 rookie class saw extended action in last Monday's 23-20 home loss to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers in Week 10. They are in an AFC North division in which every other team has a record above .500, and after falling to 4-6, they deservedly sit at the bottom of the standings heading into next week.
Drafted and undrafted first-year players saw extensive playing time in all three phases. The only rookies who were healthy scratches were fourth-round wide receiver Elijah Sarratt and fifth-round cornerback Chandler Rivers, while undrafted free agent Joe Fagnano was active, serving as the primary backup. Fifth-round running back Adam Randall wasn't activated from short-term injured reserve in his final week of eligibility. Seventh-round defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny is on the practice squad and has yet to be elevated.
Here’s an overview of how these rookies performed in their late taste of NFL regular-season action.
In his second game back after missing just one week with an MCL sprain, the first-round interior offensive lineman didn't finish the game due to a shoulder injury. Ioane played 52% of the Ravens' total snaps on offense and struggled in pass protection before being replaced for the final 33 by veteran Chuma Edoga, who had some nice reps.
Jacoby Brissett limped off the field after Vega Ioane got pushed back into his knee. pic.twitter.com/Sepv0ITBHm
The second-rounder saw a reduction in his playing time on defense for the second week in a row, with his 15 snaps in that phase of the game being the second-lowest of the season (despite the run-heavy approach) and his 11 on special teams being a new career high. Young wasn't nearly as stout setting the edge against the run as he's been for most of the season, although he did set back the Chargers' offense by 15 yards when he drew an unsportsmanlike penalty from veteran guard Cole Strange in the second quarter.
The third-round rookie was given more chances than any other pass catcher on the team to make plays through the air, with a game-high 11 targets. While he made a few nice ones for big gains, Lane also let other chances to create momentum-shifting plays slip through or bounce off his hands. On the Ravens' second drive of the third quarter, facing a third-and-long from the Los Angeles 17-yard line, he couldn't corral an on-target pass from quarterback Jacoby Brissett that would've put the ball at least at the two-yard line, and he might've even scored if his momentum had carried him into the end zone.
On the Ravens' final desperation heave of the game, just one play after Lane recorded his third catch for 21 yards, he found himself with an opportunity to make the game-winning play on a Hail Mary, but he didn't adjust to the slightly underthrown ball to make a contested catch, and the nearest defensive back batted it down instead. Lane still finished with a career-high 61 receiving yards on three catches, two of which went for first downs.
Big play to Ja'Kobi Lane!! Tune in on ESPN! pic.twitter.com/DyMFcWPTom
The fourth-rounder played exclusively on offense for the second time in his last three appearances but didn't record a single reception or even have a target come his way in 22 offensive snaps, and much like the offensive line, he didn't get much done as a run-blocker either.
The fifth-rounder played his second-fewest offensive snaps since Week 2, with 11, but that didn't stop him from having a profound impact on the offense. Cuevas helped extend the Ravens' second scoring drive of the first half late in the second quarter by hauling in all three of his targets for 37 receiving yards. All three of his snags went for first downs as the offense was able to tack a field goal on the board. Cuevas finished as the Ravens' highest-graded rookie and second-highest on offense, according to Pro Football Focus , with an overall grade of 82.2.
Jacoby Brissett and Josh Cuevas moving the Ravens down the field 👏 LACvsBAL on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Ait7LGq3aR
The sixth-round specialist had an inconsistent performance that began with a shank on his first punt that went out of bounds after only traveling 35 yards, giving the Chargers good field position to start with. He had a touchback on his longest punt of 58 yards and averaged 49.4 yards on five boots, and on the second of the two occasions, the Ravens' punt coverage units allowed a return of 20-plus yards; Eckley was forced to make his first career solo tackle.
The undrafted free agent saw a sharp reduction in playing time on defensive snaps with 13, which was his fewest since Week 6. However, he did play a career-high 25 snaps on special teams, where he made his most impactful play. On the Ravens' first kickoff of the game in the second quarter, he forced his first career fumble after securing a solo open-field tackle of former Ravens speedy running back Keaton Mitchell.
Ethan Burke is making plays in primetime 🤘 @InsideTexas pic.twitter.com/MAKTZFvdgY

title: How Much Can Rookie "Joker" Adam Randall Help The Ravens? More Than You Might Think
full_text:
The Ravens cannot get much worse, offensively.
Down to a bottom-level offensive line (that should be shuffled significantly if rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle wants to give his unit a fighting chance) that has undermined Hall of Fame running back Derrick Henry to the point where more Justice Hill (and a touch of speed) is clearly in order. The under-center run game is over (2.7 yards/carry the last six weeks) and outside zone with Henry is getting jumped before the running back gets the ball and Jacoby Brissett, the fourth starting QB this season, can’t offer enough burst and mobility to bail Doyle out on the ground.
So it’s time to see what rookie Adam Randall can do added to this mix, it’s about time he was activated from Injured Reserve and he needs a long look in a broken offense before the Ravens head to an offseason that is already littered with needs; running back among them, but to what degree? Baltimore’s brutal cap situation (worst in the NFL) means they need as many contributors on cheap entry-level contracts as possible, and what they have tried to this point in the running-back game (3.7 yards per carry during the five-game losing streak and 15 runs for 16 yards Monday against the then-winless Chargers) means it’s time to experiment and adjust.
We explained in the summer why Doyle was attracted to this hybrid offensive player at the end of the fifth round, because his primary mentor, Broncos coach Sean Payton, had a man-crush on him in Denver and spent abundant time with multiple private workouts and evaluating the Clemson product, believing his skillset as a receiver and halfback (for his final season), plus what he flashed on special teams and as a former high-school QB made him a perfect candidate to be a “Joker” who toggles between interior duties and in space and can be a bowling ball against smaller defenders on outside and win as a receiver on the inside against bigger bodies.
Randall flashed good stuff as a runner – though he is raw in that regard – early in the preseason before picking up his first injury, and he’s barely been seen since. Owner Steve Bisciotti was credited with making this pick , and with so many players failing to make an impact in this offense – pretty much everyone except for Zay Flowers and Lamar Jackson – Randall is worthy of some attention in the game plan.
Payton lit up when I brought up Randall when he joined me on “The Daily Flock” in the offseason to discuss Doyle’s offense and what to expect. He absolutely envisioned Randall as a Joker and believed he could make an impact in a stylized role as a rookie if handled appropriately.
“We ran him through certain running back drills and then we put him in space, and we put him in tight-end drills and F drills,” Payton explained. “I think his superpower is his receiving ability. So I would say, I don’t know what they’re going to list him as (on the roster in terms of playing position) and I wouldn’t be concerned with that, alright …
“With Randall, you’re going to see a player that receives the ball extremely well. We didn’t have the vision of handing the ball off to him 25 or 30 times, but we had the vision of this guy definitely being more in that F mode. If you just watched his greatest hits as a receiver, those were impressive. And then the move to halfback was really based on what they needed, and he obviously did a great job with that.
“But I’m glad you brought him up, because he was a little pet cat for us during the draft, particularly for me … So we had a vision for him as well. I wasn’t surprised at all to see that selection. I was kind of happy for Declan and Baltimore.”
Doyle has success in the screen game with Henry early in the season but that has dried up and this line couldn’t even hold up on short passes against the Chargers (15 touches for 20 scrimmage yards for Henry). Getting into more pony package looks with Hill and Randall or Flowers and Randall might help the short-passing game, and Brissett proved very willing to feature Hill in the pass game in his first game at the helm; more RB passes as potential layups would make a lot of sense.
Finding creative ways to get the ball in Randall’s hands to start seeing what he can do should be a point of emphasis moving forward.

title: 6 Winners and 6 Losers From Ravens' Inexcusable Loss To Chargers
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fifth straight game this season in Week 10 on Monday night because they weren't able to beat the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers, who held on late to notch their first victory, 23-20.
They entered this game as favorites after a mini bye, despite being on their fourth starting quarterback this season. It was supposed to be their get-back-on-track game, but they ended up serving that role for the Chargers, who looked like the most inept team in the league through the first nine weeks of the season.
With the loss, they fell to 4-6 and remain in last place in the division and have better odds of earning a top 10 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft than they do returning to the postseason with six games left to play.
Here are several Ravens players and coaches who stepped up and showed out, and others who made some costly mistakes from coaching and execution standpoints.
The second-year pro has been the only player on the team on either side of the ball who is playing their best on a consistent basis right now. Not only did Green have the first multi-sack game of his career with two and now leads the team with 5.5 on the season, but he continued to make plays and flash as a stout run defender on the edge as well, finishing with six total tackles, including four solos and two for a loss.
Mike Green with his second sack of the night!! Tune in on ESPN. pic.twitter.com/Fc2z4mw4vQ
Considering he had less than two weeks since being brought in via trade and got next to nothing from the Ravens' putrid rushing attack, what the 11-year veteran journeyman showed in his debut was nothing short of fantastic. After some initial rust and jitters, Brissett calmed down and got into rhythm and was forced to put the entire offense on his back and nearly led them to a comeback win. He completed 33-of-49 passes for 340 passing yards and delivered even more accurate passes that were tipped away or dropped.
Jacoby Brissett was impressive last night, especially considering he was pressured on 27 DROPBACKS. He set protections, alerted pressures, stayed calm in the pocket, worked through his reads well and extended a few plays. The arm was live, and he was accurate. pic.twitter.com/jEJ1Rictwc
Before he stuck his foot in his mouth by spewing disparaging remarks about the city of Baltimore on his podcast and got himself suspended for this upcoming game , the former two-time First Team All Pro actually had a nice bounce-back game. Humphrey forced a fumble on the Chargers' opening drive of the game, made some nice plays in coverage and was the Ravens' highest-graded defender and second-highest player overall, according to Pro Football Focus , with an overall of 82.4.
The former three-time Pro Bowler had his best and most productive game of the season. He served as Brissett's most reliable and sure-handed target in a passing game, two traits he hadn't been associated with all year. Andrews caught all eight of his targets for a team-leading 82 receiving yards and was the team's highest-graded player with an overall grade of 87.4.
Mark Andrews making big catches tonight 🙌 LACvsBAL on ESPN Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/KT2IJPUfkc
The sixth-year veteran didn't finish second or third on the team in receiving yards, but his contributions were just as clutch as any other pass catcher on the team in this game. Bateman caught three of his five targets for 42 receiving yards, including a 24-yard catch that set the offense up with a first-and-goal from the Los Angeles two-yard line.
The late-round rookie accounted for just over 45% of the Ravens' yardage on their second scoring drive of the game just before halftime to cut the Chargers' lead to a single possession. Cuevas caught all three of his targets for 37 receiving yards and finished as the team's second-highest-graded offensive player with an overall grade of 82.2.
While they provided Brissett with some decent pockets to throw and operate from at times, their pass protection wasn't consistently solid, and their run-blocking was so poor it was essentially non-existent . The Ravens had zero net rushing yards at halftime and finished with just 16 yards as a team on 15 carries, averaging a pitiful 1.1 yards per carry. Brissett was sacked twice, hit nine times and was forced to throw several passes away because of the pressure bearing down on him at times, especially in some key high-leverage moments.
The Ravens fared as worse in the trenches on the other side of the ball. What makes the lackluster performance of the defensive linemen just as, if not even more, inexcusable is that it came against a young and inexperienced Chargers team that was playing rookies at three of the five starting spots. They got absolutely bullied in the ground game, allowing Los Angeles to rush for a season-high 160 yards and nearly five yards per carry.
The two-time Pro Bowler was having quite the resurgent performance after back-to-back quiet games and would've been listed alongside winners if he hadn't committed yet another costly late fumble in a primetime home game. Flowers finished with six catches for 74 receiving yards, and it would've been more had he just gotten out of bounds after picking up 15 yards and getting the ball past midfield.
Despite coming off a mini-bye and claiming they did a lot of self-reflection and scouting, the Ravens looked ill-prepared to take on what was previously the worst team in the league, a mantle that they might very well be deserving of after this latest debacle. They had no answer for the quarterback run game as Justin Herbert averaged 7.3 yards per carry and racked up 51 yards and a touchdown on seven carries. Minter's unit was the first not to force Herbert to turn the ball over at least once in a game all season and failed to generate a turnover of any kind for the fourth time this season in a game they should've won and couldn't afford to lose.
Even with the two goal-line touchdowns he scored in this game, it was still another rough outing for the Future Hall of Famer, who remains on pace for the worst year of his career since becoming a bell cow at the position. He ran the ball 10 times for just 10 yards and caught a season-high five targets for just 20 yards, as almost every time he touched the ball, there was one or multiple defenders bearing down on his legs before he could build a modicum of downhill momentum.
The third-round rookie was the Ravens' most targeted pass catcher in this game with a team-leading 11 targets. While he finished with a career-high 61 receiving yards on just three catches, including a long of 31 yards, he missed some opportunities to make big plays that likely would've changed the outcome of the game.

title: 3 Statements From Rookie Coordinator Declan Doyle Reveal Why Ravens Run Game Stinks
full_text:
The Ravens’ run game is in crisis mode.
Schematic and personnel changes are in order, including less Derrick Henry and more of a speed approach on the perimeter. The offensive line is a mess and, if this team was a meritocracy, there would be at least three changes being made on that five-man unit as well (like these ). And rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has made plenty of mistakes trying to figure out life without MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson, taking his lumps in the football world about having string-bean rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane trying to crack on bulldozing edge rusher Khalil Mack on the first play of the game Monday night for a predictable loss for Henry (it was a major talking point when he met the media Thursday .
There is a lot to clean up in a lost season if the Ravens (4-6) are going to break a five-game slide and restore any semblance of balance and promise to this campaign. Doyle seems far removed from the heady days of August when he was being proclaimed a “genius” by players and a lot has been asked of him with constantly shuffling quarterbacks and an ever-changing offensive line. Carolina is 27th in run defense Expected Points Added, so another poor showing Sunday and it’s further proof that the problems rest within the Ravens roster.
Three of Doyle’s responses Thursday seemed quite revealing and telling about where his head is as the season slips away and it becomes tougher and tougher to create positive plays and winning scripts, and as his ability to position the team to succeed in the second-half of games gets called into greater question , along with rookie head coach Jesse Minter on the defensive side of the ball.
Here’s what he said, and here’s what it means:
“We're going to hang the sign that says 'physical, detailed, explosive' and physical's No. 1 there,” Doyle said. “And that's us playing fundamentally sound with pad level and coming off the ball with cadence and all those things. I felt like they beat us up physically, and that was just the bottom line.
“There's no sugarcoating that. That's what showed up on tape, and the tape is the truth. So, we have to play better. This will always be a fundamental game. It will always go back to pad level, get off, being able to utilize technique, being able to communicate, utilize double teams and things like that. That really is what we're working toward, and that's the emphasis.”
What It Mean s: He was scared to run the ball. He could have either adopted an uber-jumbo philosophy and gone with multiple tight ends and an extra offensive lineman, and tried to operate that way on the ground or through the air, and instead he thought it was a better idea to have a brand-new quarterback, Jacoby Brissett, drop back 50 times in his debut. Problem is his tackles were getting obliterated. Doyle has some of the wrong defaults and better right them, quickly.
“When you look at that kind of defense, the best avenue is generally to go outside of it – at least to start the game – and try to soften those edges,” Doyle said. “Soften it up, and then you start to create a little more space on the inside. So, that was one where Jak is our most physical blocker in that crack scheme. That's a play that we ran against Atlanta a few weeks back, and it was a successful play.
“So, really, you're trying to attack the defense. You're trying to start the game off with a run and trying to get Derrick [Henry] out in space, which is something that – as you watch the self-scout – that's something that he does really well. And it just so happens, like Khalil plays out; it gets strung out, and it ends up being a negative play. And anytime that happens, you go back to the drawing board, and you say, 'I failed as a play-caller on that play, because I didn't put him in position to have success.
What It Means: He is entirely too cute here. The Ravens are a terrible team running the ball with RBs out of 11 personnel, Brissett wants to be surrounded by TEs and this OL needs all the help it can get in every aspect of play. Watching this five times, it looks like a show-off way to open the game. It’s awfully naïve. How about "softening it up" with a tight end who has more of a fighting chance?
Henry has run 51 times for just 197 yards out of 11 personnel (3.9 yards/carry) and averaged just 0.86 yards before contact when doing do. As a team their backs average 3.9/carry doing this (23rd in the NFL). It’s not a strength and with Brissett airdropped into this offense in the middle of the season, with plenty of tight ends available, this is a stretch he can’t be making.
“That is something that every week during the planning, you're trying to find ways to five-man release it,” Doyle said, “and trying to find ways to make sure the quarterback knows where he's protected. Yet at the same point in time, it's a double-edged sword, because if you release somebody and they bring a pressure, they can dictate where you throw that ball. So, it's kind of that risk-reward balance that you go through every week."
What It Means : Dude just doesn’t understand the assignment and what he is up against here. His line is garbage. Neither tackle was any good in this game, his center is getting shoved around. Doyle told you bad they were outmuscled in the run game; you think they were holding up being walked back into the quarterback. People around the league were befuddled by 50 dropbacks, period, trying to do so with incorporating as few max-protect concepts as possible in a tight, must-win game under these circumstances shows he doesn’t grasp the hand he’s been dealt.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The Ravens' Secondary Is Failing Like Never Before. Jesse Minter's New Reality Is Bleak
full_text:
The Ravens were hopeful of having a record setting defense in their first season under wunderkind defensive mind Jesse Minter.
And they are indeed doing some truly unique things on that side of the ball with the overmatched rookie head coach in place , just not the likes of which anyone could have reasonably expected. Minter was hailed as the closest thing out there to Seattle’s Super Bowl winning coach Mike Macdonald (one of the many coaches who got away from Baltimore in recent years) and anointed as a schematic savant with a particular genius for the secondary.
And his defensive backs are among the biggest disappointments in the NFL, his defense is bottom eight in the league overall and arguably the worst in the clutch among all 32 teams. It is devoid of playmakers , yet again (you mean it wasn’t all Zach Orr’s fault?)– and Kyle Hamilton, rather than ascend to Defensive Player Of The Year heights has been largely pedestrian. Hamilton’s greatest impact has been in calling out this joke of a defense week in and week out going back to Week 2’s horrible home loss to the Saints.
Looking for unprecedented performances from the Ravens secondary? How about $19M failure Marlon Humphrey finally getting deactivated after Mayor Brandon Scott issued a public statement rebuking the cornerback’s regrettable podcast remarks? Yeah, heady times indeed in Owings Mills, where it turns out Orr could coached circles around anything Minter has mustered to this point.
But let’s quantify some of these failings, and put them in their proper perspective. Because after making creating interceptions a hallmark in two seasons running he Chargers defense, top three in interception percentage, Minter cannot get one of his defensive backs in Baltimore to get their hands on a football to save their lives (or, if this was serious organization, his job).
The Ravens are the only team in the NFL that does not have a defensive back create an interception this season ( Hamilton plays more linebacker than anything else and was playing linebacker when broken back-up quarterback Tua Tagovailoa threw a ball to him rushed into duty in overtime in Atlanta).
The Ravens and Colts – arguably the worst team in football right now – are the only teams in the NFL that do not have an interception from a cornerback.
Mind you, everyone playing the most in the Ravens’ secondary is either at the top of the pay-scale at their position, or a former first-round pick of failure GM Eric DeCosta … or both. There are supposed to be no weak links, yet instead there is no discernable strength from a playmaker standpoint (same on virtually every defense DeCosta ever built ).
Their slot coverage remains the dregs of the NFL, allowing a 123.4 passer rating (30th) as we have been documenting all season. They are the only team in the NFL without an interception on a pass to the slot. And these aren’t just layups; Baltimore is allowing 9.2 yards/attempt in the slot, 25th in the NFL.
The Ravens are allowing an opposing passer rating of 116.4 in the second half of games, second worst in the NFL (despite facing mostly bad passing offenses). They have allowed 1278 passing yards in the second half of games (30th), with 10 touchdown passes to no interceptions (worst ratio in the NFL). They paid aging designated pass rusher Trey Hendrickson’s $60M guaranteed for two years to be their “closer” but he has five pressures in the fourth quarter all season and has been ineffective all around since finger surgery in early October.
Only eight teams in the NFL have allowed more completions of 25+ yards than the Ravens, despite Minter selling out to take that away above and beyond everything else. He plays all that dime coverage and zones everything up and has resorted to doubling his use of Cover-3 during this five-game slump, but even that isn’t working. The pre-snap subterfuge is out the window and even rudimentary looks can’t get stops.
The Ravens are giving up an average of two passes of 25+ per game over the last sex weeks. That’s failure by any standard, and given Minter’s philosophy, it’s begging questions about his ability to perform either of the jobs he was hired to do .

title: Ravens Finally Discipline Struggling CB Marlon Humphrey For Podcast Remarks
full_text:
Ravens head coach Jesse Minter has been talking about standards and accountability throughout a miserably lost season, and he finally backed it up Thursday.
The rookie coach, overmatched to this point 10 games into his job, announced that $19M corner Marlon Humphrey (who carries the highest cap hit at his position in the NFL despite a credible case to be released or dealt after a terrible 2026 season ) was sent home, will not practice with the team and will not play Sunday at Carolina. Humphrey, overpaid and propped up as a “leader” on this team, has been rankling players and coaches for years with his podcasting and social-media proclivities, and his remarks on his podcast caught up to him this week.
Mayor Brandon Scott released a statement Wednesday condemning Humphrey’s comments after he asserted Baltimore is "best at making criminals ” on his podcast. Humphrey was allowed to practice and meet the media Wednesday after releasing the pod, but on Thursday Minter announced there would actually be some discipline attached.
Minter said of his communications with the former Pro Bowl player – who was a bottom 10 corner in the NFL last season – “the conversations are very, very personal and private, and to me need to remain that.”
There was every reasonable football reason to be made to pay Humphrey $4M to leave in the offseason (given his bonus structure), but he is a favorite of general manager Eric DeCosta, who rose to his defense before the season began and proclaimed him to be a “$19M corner.” And Humphrey has been picked on by bad quarterbacks and exposed by blocking tight ends in coverage. A legion of former coaches, players and execs have come on “The Daily Flock Show” including Wink Martindale, Marty Hurney, Ryan Clark, Bucky Brooks pointing out Humphrey needed a limited role in the slot, but players making $19M with a powerful font office and a rookie head coach don’t end up benched or “relegated” to the slot.
Instead, Humphrey was repeatedly allowed to take on top receivers all season and he remains as targeted as any corner in the NFL. The Ravens front office has been pushing a narrative about young corner TJ Tampa for years but he’s barely seen the field even with Humphrey struggling, though he and veteran Chidobe Awuzie will see more action Sunday now
Defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver – who vowed Humphrey and linebacker Roquan Smith would have huge bounce-back seasons and prove people wrong this spring – said on Thursday, “we love him,” about Humphrey, while pointing out how regrettable his remarks were, even in gest.
Weaver pointed to “technique and fundamentals” as key issues in Humphrey’s poor season and also noted it’s hardy been limited to him. “Defensively, we haven’t lived up to our standard,” Weaver said. This is another new low in a lost season full of them.
The Ravens have a bottom-eight defense in the NFL despite Minter being hailed as a genius on that side of the ball, and they have allowed the fifth-most points in the NFL. Minter began publicly expressing the need for locker room leadership by October, and Humphrey has been called into question in that regard for years.
The Ravens are the worst second-half team in the NFL, Baltimore does not have a second-half interception and they do not have an interception from a corner or safety in coverage all season (Kyle Hamilton’s came as a linebacker), despite Minter’s zone coverages being hailed as exemplary in that regard. Minter is being viewed around the NFL as a potential one-and-done head coach if he cannot quickly stop this rot after five straight defeats, all embarrassing in their own way.
DeCosta has said not addressed the media since telling Ravens fans why Humphrey was worth $19M a season and how optimistic he was about signing Lamar Jackson back before this brutal season began.

title: Should Jesse Minter Relinquish Play-Calling Duties? NFL Analyst Ryan Clark Believes So
full_text:
Struggling Ravens rookie head coach Jesse Minter was dismissive when questioned last week about relinquishing defensive play-calling duties amid his team’s collective failures. He should not have been.
There is a certain ego and hubris involved in performing that task for him – and ego and hubris have got the franchise into an ugly mess in all aspects of the organization – but Minter, soon enough, is going to see that the big picture of him trying to establish himself as anything close to an NFL head coach may require divesting himself of some duties. Longtime Raiders team president Amy Trask believes it must be on the table, and longtime NFL safety and NFL analyst Ryan Clark thinks the same thing.
Baltimore’s defense is a shell of what it was supposed to be.
The coverage is terrible, the pass rush is barely-pedestrian, they produce no turnovers or big plays and they have been the worst in the NFL in the second half. They blew double-digit leads with regularity back when the offense was good enough to build them (before Lamar Jackson got hurt) and lately they have been getting torn up in the first quarter of games to fall too far behind for the back-up QBs to have a chance.
Minter has not found the ability to motivate these players or make anything close to sage in-game adjustments in any aspect of play, bringing up questions of this being a potential one-and-done scenario should a five-game losing streak spill into December. Yes, calling plays on defense got him this job, but he’s become one of the worst coordinators in the NFL trying to wear both hats, and something has to give as players continue to say and do ridiculous things on their podcasts on the field of play with no accountability to this point.
It’s a dichotomy Minter better get his head around, fast.
Clark, who joined “The Daily Flock Show”’ this week, believes Minter needs to rely more on coordinator Anthony Weaver on game-day; Weaver is a former NFL player with a long coaching history on the defensive line and calling defenses himself.
“You say to yourself, this was the thing I was really good at,” Clark said of Minter calling plays. “And because I was really good at that thing, I want to continue doing that because that gives me something on game day I can control outside of delegation.
“So, I don't know if he should pull it back. What I do know is when I watched Miami play under Anthony Weaver defensively, Miami knew they sucked, right? No, they did … There was no secret. They were terrible. But their defense played hard as hell … They ran and they hit and they pressured ... Maybe, maybe giving Anthony Weaver that sort of control over the defense would help.
“Because no matter what, even though I see Anthony Weaver in the room every week, I know he's not the guy, right? Like, we got a different relationship cuz this is the guy. And so maybe him relinquishing that to (Weaver) would probably feel like I failed as a defensive coordinator here and I'm removing myself because I failed. Hopefully he would be able to see it as I'm not failing. I'm giving someone who I trust the power to make a difference on game day so I can now fully focus on this job I've earned.”
Clark, like many others, believes Minter has watered down his approach and shunned pre-snap masking just hoping to sit in a shell and take away big plays. Even that isn’t working. The standard has fallen so low, that just getting guts to run to the football and wrap up as tacklers has been too tall a task at times. Instead of Kyle Hamilton moving all over in a role where no one knows what he’s doing, Clark sees him just standing around at the line of scrimmage “90% of the time.”
It’s not bringing out the best in anyone (except linebacker Trenton Simpson ), and other teams are picking on the weak links with abandon.
“I see it on film; other teams see it on film,” Clark said. “What adjustment is Anthony Weaver and Jesse Mentor making to get it right? And, yes, players got to make plays, but I also schematically I earned this job because of my success as a defensive coach. Where are the adjustments?
“We saw Mike Macdonald make those adjustments and become a head coach in Seattle, right? When are they going to make that adjustment with this iteration of the Baltimore Ravens?"
My best guess is - not this season.
Clark described it as a simplistic defense at this point. That might be kind. Teams attack corner Marlon Humphrey from the jump every week, there isn’t enough pressure on opposing quarterbacks, and Minter should be feeling the heat.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Three Changes Ravens Rookie Offensive Coordinator Declan Doyle Must Make Now
full_text:
The Ravens' season has slipped away, Lamar Jackson may have thrown his last pass for the franchise and the team’s young coordinators have much to prove in games that won’t matter much come January.
All the talk about 30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle being a “genius” from this summer has subsided, he cannot figure out a way to run the ball whatsoever right now to the point where overmatched rookie head coach Jesse Minter seems more frustrated about that than anything else, and general manager Eric DeCosta handed him an offensive line that is truly atrocious and is the kind of thing that would get people fired in an organization in which the owner was engaged and cunning.
Evaluating Doyle is more difficult given how jaundiced this prism has become – no Jackson (and maybe no Jackson ever again , as Ryan Clark explained), no pass protection, no holes in the run game, only one receiver who wins downfield. Honestly, what Minter has been unable to do on the defensive side should be giving massive pause to everyone in The Castle beyond some of these offensive struggles, but it’s fair to wonder if Jackson is the only thing close to a genius in that building and this is a four-win team , at best, without him, with or without Doyle calling the plays.
Still, there is pressure on this young staff and Doyle must take some tangible and obvious measures to try to derive a modicum of balance and some element of surprise from an offense that is woefully lacking in that regard. As always, we have some cogent suggestions for him:
My buddy Marty Hurney, longtime general manager and admittedly old-school, was going to pull his hair out talking to me about Baltimore’s offense this week and the decision to drop back 50 times with Jacoby Brissett in his first game with the team in Monday’s loss to the previously-winless Chargers.
“You have to be willing to stick with the run and give it a chance to work,” he intoned. “It’s the whole league, man! It’s not just the Ravens.”
One way to help that cause is to dedicate to personnel groupings that can help a terrible line have a fighting chance. We’ve documented the woes of the run game – and the case for more Justice Hill ( at length here ) – but Baltimore is averaging a gaudy 5.4 yards/rush when it utilizes an extra offensive lineman. Doesn’t matter if the other team knows it’s a run; Doyle has to commit to it.
The Ravens also got out of their 13 personnel (three tight end) looks when blocker Durham Smythe was lost for the season but it needs to come back. Doyle has no wide receivers who win on the outside anyway and rookie Ja’Kobi Lane is getting funneled and is struggling right now and the tight ends are more trustworthy and Jacoby Brissett threw a higher percentage of passes to TE in two years in Arizona than anyone in the NFL; and the Cardinals are second in the NFL in usage of 13 this season, so the QB is accustomed to it.
The Ravens went from using 13 over 16% of the time in the first six weeks to just 9.7% since Week 7. Doyle needs to ramp it up. Keep Josh Cuevas involved and get Matthew Hibner going and Nick Vannett is a blocking option and they have a fullback to use more, too.
What’s the point of having Elijah Sarratt inactive every week as fourth-round receiver on a bad football team going nowhere? Even cutting back on the 11 personnel as I am calling for,  we seriously prefer Chris Moore to him (even with Moore on special teams?). We can’t coach Sarratt up on teams and get him at least blocking?
Hibner needs a run on seam routes. We documented how poorly many individuals are on this offensive line are performing , and want to see Carson Vinson at tackle. Doyle had the temerity to fall back on “player development” for not playing Smythe as much he should have back in Week 2, so let’s see the kid TEs now.
Remember when Doyle said he was going to dabble with calling games from the sidelines and the press box and then make up his mind? Then he had a great game against the Eagles fourth stringers in a preseason game upstairs and never came down. Might be time for a rethink.
Yeah, let’s mix it up, rook.
Doyle seems too disconnected from the action to me and part of why these QBs are getting hung out to dry by weird play calling behind a bad line might be because he isn’t seeing things at ground level like he should. He has a lot of new parts and a new offensive line every week and wants to script the entire game from the jump. That's not how it works.
He gave this a run, it’s been a disaster without Jackson, and he needs to take a different tact.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Key Linebacker Injury Gives Bills' Rookie Fourth-Rounder Shot to Shine vs. Dolphins
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills ' final injury report for their Week 11 matchup against the Miami Dolphins was released on Friday, and one of the inactives presents an opportunity for an under-the-radar member of the Bills' rookie class.
Starting linebacker Dorian Williams was ruled out for Sunday's contest with a calf injury, which should thrust fourth-round pick Kaleb Elarms-Orr into a starting role opposite veteran Terrel Bernard.
While Miami does not look like a challenging opponent, a strong outing from the TCU product will go a long way toward ensuring this game is not a trap game with a gauntlet awaiting them starting Thursday.
The Bills do a good job surrounding the ball in space, and Kaleb Elarms-Orr (52) delivers a SHOT at point of contact pic.twitter.com/EBEriPBQwA
Out of Buffalo's 600 defensive snaps in 2026, Elarms-Orr has seen the field in 126, or 21%, of them, working behind Williams and Bernard and fighting with Joe Andreessen for the right to see the field.
Statistically, the rookie has tallied 18 tackles, a pass defended and two fumble recoveries, showcasing his athleticism in spurts, but he'll have a chance to make himself known to Bills Mafia in front of the Highmark Stadium crowd on Sunday.
In the preseason, Elarms-Orr tallied six tackles and turned heads in training camp, most notably by starting a fight that drew the attention of veterans, including guard Alec Anderson.
"Shoutout to the rookie linebacker Kaleb [Elarms-Orr]," Anderson said after the fight. "You'd rather say 'chill' than 'sic 'em'... that's a good thing."
Coming out of college, Elarms-Orr was praised for his athleticism, which included a 4.47 40-yard dash, a 40-inch vertical jump and a 4.41 shuttle run, and college production, as he l ed the Big 12 with 130 tackles in 2025.
“Elarms-Orr is a well-built linebacker with above-average athleticism but problematic instincts,” NFL.com ’s Lance Zierlein wrote. “He has the speed and athleticism to get to the football from sideline to sideline.”
The Hayward, California native will need to combine his speed with improved instincts if he is to help Buffalo shut down Miami's playmakers.
Elarms-Orr will be relieved to not go up against running back De'Von Achane, who ran for 1,350 yards, good for fifth in the league, and also led the Dolphins with 67 receptions. Achane tore his ACL in Week 3 against the Kansas City Chiefs.
Second-year running back Ollie Gordon II, Achane's replacement, has run for at least 100 yards in two of six games since Achane's injury, and the running game will be key for Miami if it is to keep the ball away from Josh Allen and the Bills' offense.
When quarterback Kyle McCord drops back to throw , tight end Greg Dulcich, who has 24 catches for 270 yards this season, will be his main responsibility.
With a short week coming up, a strong performance from Elarms-Orr could be exactly what the Bills welcome.

title: Bills' Final Week 11 Injury Report: Two Defensive Starters Out, TE Dalton Kincaid Doubtful
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills ' final Week 11 injury report contained a mixture of disappointment and positive developments.
While the defense will be without starting cornerback Christian Benford and inside linebacker Dorian Williams, who were ruled out on Friday, when the Bills host the Miami Dolphins for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff on November 22, two other starters were cleared for action.
After sustaining injuries last time out against the New York Jets on November 15, slot  cornerback Dee Alford and safety Cole Bishop do not carry a designation into Sunday.
Alford cleared the concussion protocol in only five days while Bishop, who is fighting through a shoulder issue, managed to record back-to-back days of full practice participation.
Going back to Benford and Williams, Bills' head coach Joe Brady delivered an encouraging nugget on their status by dismissing the idea that either player will be out for the long term. Benford has an injured groin while Williams deals with a calf strain.
Meanwhile, safety Damar Hamlin and defensive lineman TJ Sanders are both questionable to face the Dolphins in Week 11.
Hamlin, who was seen in a walking boot using a mobility scooter earlier in the week, missed back-to-back practices due to a toe. He returned in a limited capacity on Friday. Sanders, who has been nursing a shoulder issue, was downgraded from full to limited on Thursday.
While the offense is about as healthy as one can expect at this point in the season, there is a potential problem at tight end.
Starter Dalton Kincaid, one of the offense's top pass-catchers, did not practice this week. As a result, he's officially doubtful to play .
Complicating matters for a team that likes to deploy up the three tight ends at the same time, third-stringer Jackson Hawes is questionable due to a shoulder issue. He was limited throughout the practice week while wearing a red non-contact jersey.
Meanwhile, Kincaid is now dealing with a thumb injury in addition to the ankle issue that originated in Week 9 .
"He's playing a lot. We're doing a lot in 13 personnel, 11 personnel [formations] and I think some of the bumps and bruises are naturally gonna come," said Brady on Friday .
The thumb issue emerged during a third-quarter red zone play against the New York Jets in Week 10. He engaged down field with linebacker Demario Davis, seemingly jamming the thumb in the process.
"I think it's frustrating for anybody when there's a possibility that you can miss a game. We put so much on our tight ends' plates that no one's gonna feel perfect at this time of the year," said Brady.
Should Kincaid and Hawes be unable to go, the Bills would be left with only two tight ends — Dawson Knox and Keleki Latu.
In a positive development for the offense, backup running back Ray Davis was upgraded to full participation on Friday. He was limited by a hamstring on Wednesday and Thursday.
While cornerback Maxwell Hairston will presumably start opposite second-round rookie Davison Igbinosun, the Bills have no other true outside cornerbacks on the 53-man roster.
Although Alford can flip outside if need be, Buffalo seems best served by making a practice squad elevation with veteran Tre'Davious White and undrafted rookie Kani Walker both viable options.
When it comes to plugging the hole created by Williams's absence, fourth-round rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr becomes the presumed starter after filling in the rest of the way against the Jets . That makes Joe Andreessen the primary backup with a practice squad elevation likely, too.

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Miami Dolphins Week 11 Expert Pick Roundup
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have been handling their business this season . They've had some bounces go their way as they have faced backup quarterbacks against the Baltimore Ravens, Minnesota Vikings, and New York Jets but they can't control who they play. All they can control is how they play, and they've played well enough to enter Week 11 with a record of 8-1.
They're also facing yet another backup this weekend . With Malik Willis out, the Miami Dolphins will start former Syracuse quarterback Kyle McCord . As if that wasn't enough adversity for Miami, they will also be without star running back De’Von Achane.
With that being the case, the Bills are heavy favorites in this one. That's why it should be no surprise at all to see their name as the primary selection in our latest expert pick roundup.
With 30 experts making a selection across these media outlets, the Bills stand out as the overwhelming favorites to pick up the win at home.
It might seem surprising to see seven selections for the Dolphins, but to be fair, those picks were all made against the spread. Those writers are saying the game will be closer than the odds indicate, not necessarily that Miami will win.
As for my prediction, it's hard to see this turning into anything other than a blowout win for the Bills. They're at home, their defense has been playing much better in recent weeks, and the Dolphins are playing a quarterback with one career start. Miami's defense has been better than it gets credit for this season, but the Bills are simply too good not to win this one by multiple scores. Look for both James Cook and Josh Allen to have big games on the ground while Jim Leonhard's defense has another stellar game.

title: Bills' Undrafted WR Ready for Action vs. Dolphins After Beating Odds Again
full_text:
He spent nearly two full seasons on the Buffalo Bills ' practice squad before even getting a sniff of real NFL action .
When he finally played in his first career playoff game mote than 2.5 years after signing an undrafted free agent rookie contract, wide receiver Tyrell Shavers tore his ACL.
Remarkably, Shavers remained active for the entire second half of the wildcard road win over the Jacksonville Jaguars after suffering the devastating knee injury prior to halftime.
Obviously, surgery and an intense  rehabilitation process followed, but Shavers worked back into form in just about 10 months' time.
His relatively quick return for a wide receiver is another example of beating long odds. Shavers began his collegiate career at Alabama pre-COVID before transferring to Mississippi State. He eventually landed at San Diego State.
"He's got one of the best stories out there," said quarterback Josh Allen. "Just how he bounced around in college, coming here, being a P-squad guy, not really getting opportunities, and finally getting his opportunities, and making the most of them. Getting injured, fighting back, and now he's back out here practicing."
His first official practice was on October 28 as the Bills opened his 21-day activation window.
Needing to add him to the 53-man roster this week, or lose him for the remainder of the season, Buffalo created a roster spot for Shavers on Monday when it sent seventh-round rookie offensive guard Ar'maj Reed-Adams to Injured Reserve.
Shavers was a full participant at practice this week, seemingly aiming to make his season debut when the Miami Dolphins visit Orchard Park for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff on November 22.
"The hope is that he'll be up [on Sunday], but a lot of that has to do with, there's a lot of roster moves with some of the injuries and stuff that kind of play into it," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady on Friday afternoon .
Last week, the Bills dressed five wide receivers, including return specialist Greg Dortch and fourth-round rookie Skyler Bell. It's presumed that Shavers will take Bell's game day roster spot. Bell has already been a healthy scratch six times this season.
"I think he's had a good week in practice," said Brady. "The intent and the hope is that he'll be up, but we'll see what that kinda looks like."
Shavers will likely slide in as the Bills' fourth wide receiver, and his eagerness to run block may earn him more snaps on offense.
“A lot of trust between me and him," said Allen.
As essentially a fifth wide receiver in 2025 , Shavers appeared in all 17 regular season games, including nine starts . Totaling a 39 percent snap share on offense, he made 15 receptions for 245 yards and one touchdown.
"Big body, he'll go up and get it, he'll go in and block duo [run play]. He does all the dirty work. He plays special teams. He never complains. He's where he's supposed to be at all times. He's a great teammate, so very, very happy for him to get back," said Allen.

title: Bills' Head Coach Joe Brady On Cusp of Historical Feat Not Achieved in 15 Years
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have had quite an exciting journey so far through the 2026 NFL campaign's first half under first-year head coach Joe Brady.
Sitting atop the NFL standings with an 8-1 record for the first time since the 1991 season when Hall-of-Fame head coach Marv Levy was still at the helm in Western New York, Brady has kept his team on an upward trajectory throughout this fall despite some inconsistencies seemingly continuing to pop up on a weekly basis for the club.
However, the team has never wavered in those moments of doubt, and it’s been quite the feat to watch unfold through the first nine games.
With a win on Sunday, Joe Brady can become the first rookie head coach since Jim Harbaugh with the San Francisco 49ers in 2011 to begin his coaching career with a 9-1 or better record. pic.twitter.com/wfKx52pram
And now, along with the help of his coordinators Jim Leonhard, Pete Carmichael Jr., and Jeff Rodgers, as well as former 2024 MVP quarterback Josh Allen , Brady has a chance to do something that hasn’t been seen anywhere in the National Football League—not just Orchard Park, New York—in 15 years.
And, what is that you might ask?
Well, after becoming just the fourth head coach since 2000 to begin his career 8-1 following last week’s win over the New York Jets, with a victory over the Miami Dolphins at home this week Brady can now become the first rookie head coach in the NFL to start his professional endeavor off with a 9-1 mark since current Los Angeles Chargers’ veteran coach Jim Harbaugh did so back in 2011 with the San Francisco 49ers.
Accompanied by coordinators Greg Roman ( OC ), Vic Fangio ( DC ), and Brad Seely ( Asst. HC/ST ), as well as veteran quarterback Alex Smith and legendary running back Frank Gore at the time, Harbaugh eventually led San Francisco to an overall record of 13-3 during the regular season that year before the 49ers ultimately fell to the New York Giants in overtime during the NFC Championship game by a score of 20-17 later on that January.
It was the first time since the 1997-1998 season that San Francisco had reached that far in the playoffs, and Harbaugh and Co. subsequently followed that performance up by getting into Super Bowl XLVII the next season.
In the end, however, the team lost to the Baltimore Ravens by three points in the pinnacle game at the Mercedes-Benz Superdome in New Orleans.
Nevertheless, it was still an incredible start to Harbaugh’s coaching career, and it’s likely a track that Bills Mafia members would like to see Brady’s team take this winter . . . with a different outcome at the end, of course.
Whether or not that will actually occur remains to be seen, but—given some of the “roadblocks” that still seem to be lying in their pathway to SoFi Stadium in February—Buffalo will certainly be battle tested if they do reach their desired final destination.
Ultimately, it will likely come down to whether or not the Bills’ somewhat unsteady defense can provide support for Allen and the offense in critical moments down the line, particularly in the playoffs.
Only time will tell, but it definitely seems like Bills’ fans can start thinking about partying like it’s the 1990s again.
Seeing how the AFC and NFC standings are stacking up, maybe the NFL will finally get the Chris Berman special in the Super Bowl: the 49ers vs. the Bills .

title: Christian Benford Injury News Likely Forces Bills Into Pre-Game Week 11 Roster Move
full_text:
He's been back in town for about one full month already, and he may be back in game action sooner than later .
The Buffalo Bills signed veteran cornerback Tre'Davious White to their practice squad on October 19, adding a proven insurance policy at a highly important position on defense.
Four weeks later, the Bills have a cornerback deficit with starter Christian Benford already ruled out for the November 22 home game against the Miami Dolphins.
Benford suffered a groin injury that sidelined him during the November 15 road victory over the New York Jets. As a result, he was a non-participant throughout the practice week.
While Maxwell Hairston will presumably start in Benford's place, opposite second-round rookie Davison Igbinosun, the Bills have no other true outside cornerback on the 53-man roster behind the probable Week 11 starters.
For numbers purposes alone, Buffalo likely needs to make an addition to the game day roster. The most practical move is to call up either White or undrafted rookie Kani Walker to face the Dolphins.
"If we have to have any practice squad call-ups. We feel comfortable with the guys on there," said head coach Joe Brady after Friday's practice .
Starting slot cornerback Dee Alford, who has officially cleared concussion protocol, can flip outside if needed, but his versatility can't make up for the lack of available bodies in the cornerback room.
"We have the ability with [Jordan] Hancock to be able to play inside and Dee [Alford] being able to play outside. There's a lot of options that we, obviously, are sorting through," said Brady.
The 31-year-old White, a 2017 first-round draft pick, returned to the organization in 2025 after one year away, and he unexpectedly wound up as a Week 1 starter.
White made 16 regular season starts for the Bills last year, providing a steadying presence as Hairston faced multiple obstacles during his rookie campaign.
"We brought Tre back here, if given the opportunity, to go in there and help us play winning football. I thought he played really good football at the end of last season," said Brady.
As a starter, White totaled 40 tackles, 6.0 TFL, nine pass breakups and one interception during the regular season. He limited opposing passers to a 51.1 completion percentage and 5.1 yards per attempt when targeted. In the wildcard road win over the Jacksonville Jaguars he deflected a pass that wound up as the game-clinching interception.
"I got the confidence that whenever that time does come, and Tre White has to be up, there's gonna be no holding the breath, because I know he's so calm, cool collected, he's ready to go," said Brady.
White's first practice was on October 28 as the Bills came out of their Week 7 bye.
"Anytime you kind of onboard some veteran players as the season goes on, that's part of the process is how many plays do you think you could play right now? I like where he's at," said defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard on Monday.
Even though he's only weeks removed from the couch , White, who was labeled "a freak, genetically" by Brady, is apparently in playing condition.
"I think he's really close to being able to help us. We had some injuries here this last game, if need be, I think he's ready to step up and play for us," said Leonhard.
With Benford out, it seems only right to elevate White.

title: Joe Brady's Update Deals Blow to Dalton Kincaid's Availability for Bills vs. Dolphins
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are presumably preparing to be without one of their primary pass-catchers when the Miami Dolphins visit on November 22.
For the third day in a row, the Bills held tight end Dalton Kincaid out of practice.
While addressing reporters on Friday in Orchard Park, Bills' head coach Joe Brady labeled Kincaid's Week 11 availability as doubtful. Theoretically, that designation gives the tight end around a 25 percent chance to make the active game day roster.
Kincaid hasn't missed a game yet this season. He has totaled 32 receptions for 487 yards and two touchdowns for the Bills (8-1).
Kincaid just can't seem to escape the injury report lately.
"He's playing a lot. We're doing a lot in 13 personnel, 11 personnel [formations] and I think some of the bumps and bruises are naturally gonna come," said Brady on Friday.
He encountered a ribs/chest issue on October 18 against the Las Vegas Raiders. Despite going to the locker room for evaluation, Kincaid finished the game heading into the Week 7 bye.
Kincaid practiced on a limited basis heading into the November 1 game against the Baltimore Ravens. Questionable to played, he saw 47 snaps while making four receptions for 86 yards and one touchdown.
After shaking the chest issue, Kincaid injured his ankle while blocking for DJ Moore along the sideline against the Minnesota Vikings on November 9. That wasn't enough, however, to keep him out on a short week heading into the New York Jets game .
Getting tangled up with a defender against the Jets on November 15, the thumb has become the major issue for Kincaid in Week 11.
"We're asking him to do a lot more this year," said Brady. "I think it's frustrating for anybody when there's a possibility that you can miss a game. We put so much on our tight ends' plates that no one's gonna feel perfect at this time of the year."
The thumb injury appeared to occur during a red zone play midway through the third quarter when Kincaid briefly engaged with Jets' linebacker Demario Davis about nine yards past the line of scrimmage. He eventually returned for two more plays later in the half, but his day ended early.
While Kincaid has made a habit of playing through injuries over the past few years, a bum thumb can significantly limit a pass-catcher who must double as a blocker.
The hope is for Kincaid to perform a repeat of starting right tackle Spencer Brown's feat from Week 10. Dealing with an ankle injury, Brown missed three consecutive practices and was designated as doubtful. By the time game day arrived, however, he was ready to go .
Still, the odds are leaning toward Kincaid being scratched when the Bills declare inactives 90 minutes prior to the 1 p.m. ET kickoff.

title: Six Bills Coaches Considered 'Rising NFL Names to Watch' for Future Head Coach Jobs
full_text:
Each and every year, NFL insider Tom Pelissero lists off several coaches around the league who could garner interest for head coaching vacancies down the road and this year's list has six Buffalo Bills coaches on it.
Pelissero's list is divided into two sections , with one naming all of the coaches who could receive interest in 2027, and another listing potential candidates in 2028 and beyond.
All six of the Bills coaches who were listed by Pelissero fell into the second category and were headlined by first-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard .
Here's a look at the other five:
Of all of the coaches listed, Leonhard should be considered the favorite to land a head coaching gig first, simply because he is already a defensive coordinator.
While past performance isn't the only factor teams consider when hiring a new head coach, it's definitely an important part of the equation and Leonhard doesn't have a great resume as a play-caller yet given Buffalo's struggles defensively in 2026 .
But he's still very early in the process and if he can turn things around from now through next season, it's possible teams will come calling in 2028.
Given their experience, we would peg Hardegree and Egorugwu as the Bills assistants who are most likely to get a look from teams as coordinators, which is the best path to eventually landing a head coaching gig.
Hardegree is the only coach on the list who has actually served as an offensive or defensive coordinator when he was the interim offensive coordinator for the Las Vegas Raiders in 2023.
Egorugwu is in his second stint with the Bills after he served as the team's defensive quality control coach in 2017 and then as the assistant linebackers coach from 2018-20.
Egorugwu's NFL coaching experience dates back to 2015 and only Hardegree (2014) has been coaching in the league longer.
Terrell's NFL coaching career dates back to 2018, and on top of being a wide receivers coach, he was a passing-game coordinator in Arizona, which is a step above from just being a position coach.
The son of former NFL head coach Pat Shurmur, Kyle spent stints with Washington, the Kansas City Chiefs and Cincinnati Bengals during his playing career before moving into coaching. His NFL coaching career began in 2022 with the Bills , when he was a defensive quality control coach.
Valai's pro coaching career goes back to 2018, when the Chiefs hired him as a defensive quality control coach. He went back to college in 2019 and only re-emerged in the NFL this year.
While it remains to be seen if any of these assistants will ever get a better gig, it's at least good to see the Bills have a lot of promising coaches on their staff.

title: Bills' Training Camp Fan Favorite Earns Second Pro Opportunity, Chosen in UFL Draft
full_text:
He had a cup of coffee with the Buffalo Bills this past summer, but this rookie offensive tackle apparently isn't satisfied.
Duke product Bruno Fina, who signed an undrafted free agent contract with the Bills back in May, was amongst those players selected in the United Football League's 15-round draft that unfolded this week in St. Louis.
The UFL's Colorado Stampede picked Fina at No. 91 overall (Round 12) on Thursday.
Bruno Fina is Colorado bound 💪 pic.twitter.com/j5YT5kKyiA
This past spring, Fina instantly became a Bills Mafia fan favorite as a result of his surname. His father, John, played 10 seasons for the Bills after being chosen No. 27 overall in the 1992 NFL Draft .
Fina Sr. displayed his excitement over the news by sharing the Stampede's draft post on X. The Bills' former first-round pick knows the joys of professional football firsthand after making 160 career appearances, including 12 playoff games, for the organization that drafted him.
The 24-year-old Bills' legacy, a true roster long shot, moved inside to offensive guard during training camp. Fina appeared in all three preseason games before being waived on cutdown day .
In the exhibition opener in Orchard Park, Fina saw four snaps on offense to go along with five special teams reps against the Carolina Panthers. His snap count increased  the following week on the road against the Cleveland Browns. He logged 24 offensive reps plus five more on specials.
Fina, who spent the past two seasons as Duke's starting left tackle, did the Bills a solid in the preseason finale against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
With the Bills attempting to preserve veteran backup Lloyd Cushenberry , and starter Connor McGovern on the shelf, Fina stepped up to start at center against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Fina logged 65 snaps on offense in the 28-27 win.
Defensive back MJ Devonshire was selected by the Dallas Renegades at No. 83 overall (Round 11).
Devonshire, a 2024 seventh-round pick by the Las Vegas Raiders, signed with the Bills' practice squad last December after the team lost Ja'Marcus Ingram to the Houston Texans. Buffalo gave him a futures contract in January, but subsequently waived him in May.
Punter Jack Stonehouse was selected one pick prior to Fina, going to the Renegades at No. 90 overall.
Stonehouse, a Syracuse product, met with the Bills at the NFL Combine. He subsequently interviewed with Buffalo at their local pro day in April. The Bills, however, opted to draft Florida's Tommy Doman to compete for primary punting duties .

title: Three Keys to Bills Avoiding Trap-Game Letdown vs. Dolphins
full_text:
With a win against the Miami Dolphins at Highmark Stadium on Sunday, the Buffalo Bills will improve to 9-1 for the first time since 1991.
Thirty-five years, three additional gut-wrenching losses in the Super Bowl, and countless other heartbreakers have since occurred between when Buffalo last achieved that regular-season mark following a game against the Green Bay Packers on November 10, 1991, and now, but that doesn’t change the fact that fans and media members are drinking the Kool-Aid , so to speak, when it comes to first-year head coach Joe Brady’s chances of leading his team on a deep postseason run later on in January.
And, it’s hard to blame anyone for doing so.
Following the recent trade for veteran playmaking safety Amani Hooker, the right recipe appears to be in place for quarterback Josh Allen and the Bills to finally get over the proverbial playoff wall in a mere matter of months.
However, before anyone can really start focusing on anything past the regular season, the Western New York franchise still has plenty of business to attend to as the calendar creeps toward December.
The team’s remaining schedule is anything but easy—and very well may be the toughest slate of the whole year for Brady’s crew—so it’ll be important for Allen and Co. to stockpile as many more wins as possible against opponents like the Dolphins, which is a team still searching for its second win of the 2026 campaign under fellow rookie head coach Jeff Haffley.
With that in mind, considering that Buffalo has a primetime matchup versus the Kansas City Chiefs on tap for Thanksgiving night in Orchard Park on Thursday, is there a possibility of the Bills falling victim to the classic “trap game” on Sunday afternoon against Miami?
But, if the team wants any chance at obtaining the No. 1 seed in the AFC entering the playoffs down the road, then it’ll be crucial to avoid any such event from unfolding this weekend.
So, keeping that in mind, here are three keys to the Bills avoiding letdown against their divisional counterpart.
For the fourth consecutive game since the team’s much-needed bye week last month, Buffalo’s defense is being gifted the opportunity to face a backup quarterback instead of the opponents’ preferred option at gunslinger.
So, while it’s true that Bills’ defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s youthful unit is putting up some historically impressive numbers in recent weeks, there’s no denying that the statistics have been somewhat skewed.
However, the team can only play who’s in front of them, and so far the defensive players have been handling business in November.
That must continue on Sunday versus Dolphins’ rookie quarterback Kyle McCord, who made his first NFL start on the road last week at Lucas Oil Stadium against the Indianapolis Colts that ended in a 24-22 loss.
Regardless of the opponent, narrowly missing out on a road win in your first NFL start is impressive for any player.
And, McCord (17-of-32 for 209 yards ) did so while falling just 11 passing yards shy of breaking former Dolphins’ quarterback Ryan Tannehill’s debut passing record ( 219 yards ), which he set in 2012. He also rushed for one touchdown.
So, needless to say, while the young former Syracuse University star won’t be shell-shocked in Western New York this weekend with one road start already under his belt, it’ll be crucial that Leonhard’s cast of players make him feel unwelcomed and uncomfortable for four quarters.
Pass-rushers like Gregory Rousseau, rookie T.J. Parker, and captain Bradley Chubb, who is a former Dolphins’ defender, will need to help make sure that’s the case.
Although the Bills convincingly came out on top against the New York Jets last week with a 31-12 road victory, the team actually only possessed a four-point lead at halftime on Sunday at MetLife Stadium in case any Bills Mafia members may have forgotten.
And, despite the game never seeming to be truly in question against the Jets, Buffalo must avoid having a similar sluggish start on offense against Miami head coach Jeff Hafley and coordinator Sean Duggan’s defense this week at home.
The Dolphins recently held the Detroit Lions’ high-powered offense, which ranks fifth in the NFL in points per game this season heading into Week 11, to just 19 points back on November 8, so they’re certainly a capable unit on defense despite some inconsistencies at times.
Overall, the team is ranked 10th in total yards allowed at just 320.6 per game according to FOX Sports ' database, as well as seventh in passing yards allowed at 202.1 yards per game, so it might be more of a struggle for Allen and his group of playmakers versus Miami than some might think.
Buffalo can’t afford to let anything wonky happen this weekend, which could certainly happen if the offense can’t start the game out quickly and smoothly.
With that in mind, Allen must take what the defense gives him and not force the issue.
After recently placing veteran defensive lineman Zach Sieler on injured reserve nearly two weeks ago, as well as fellow interior defenders Zeke Biggers and Jordan Phillips on the list just on Tuesday, there’s no denying that the Dolphins are hurting up front on the defensive line entering Sunday’s matchup in the AFC East.
And, pairing that with the fact that the team is only ranked 18th in the NFL in rushing yards allowed per game to the opposition at a rate of 118.4 yards per contest on the ground, it would appear that the Bills might be hard-pressed to find a better avenue to take to exploit their divisional foe’s defense this weekend.
So, while it’s true that veteran running back James Cook’s high-usage rate might be a bit of a concern to some heading toward the latter part of the regular season, it’ll be critical that Buffalo maintain a healthy ground attack this weekend at Highmark Stadium.
Effectively keeping the clock rolling versus Miami and trying to quickly move on to Thanksgiving’s showdown with Kansas City isn’t a bad plan of attack.

title: 3 Panthers Players Who Deserve More Playing Time Against Ravens
full_text:
The Panthers got a win over New Orleans, but there is still work to do on the offensive side of the ball. Baltimore comes to Charlotte on Sunday, and Carolina needs to find a way to get more production from the players around Bryce Young.
A few players could use more chances to make an impact against the Ravens. Carolina needs another receiver to step up, and it could also use a little more help in the backfield.
Legette was back on the field Sunday after missing several games with a knee injury. He only got two offensive snaps against the Saints, and the Panthers didn't have much of a chance to work him into the game. That needs to change as he gets further removed from the injury.
Legette has the speed to make plays downfield, something Carolina could use against Baltimore. He already showed what he can do with the 55-yard catch against Atlanta before his injury. Getting him more involved would give Young another way to attack the Ravens. Legette has been eager to get back into a bigger role.
The Ravens will be without starting cornerback Marlon Humphrey and safety Jaylinn Hawkins against the Panthers. This leaves the Ravens' secondary short-handed, and the Panthers must take advantage of this. Legette can make some downfield plays for the Panthers and give Young another option to look for when he drops back to pass.
Metchie hasn't had many chances to make an impact in Carolina's offense. Against New Orleans, he was on the field for just 23 of the Panthers' 70 offensive snaps, or 33% of the team's plays. Young targeted him once, completing a short pass that gained four yards.
Carolina could use another receiver to take some attention away from McMillan and Coker. Metchie hasn't had many opportunities to show what he can do, but he has the experience to help this passing game. With Humphrey out, the Panthers have a chance to test Baltimore's secondary, and Metchie deserves more opportunities to be part of that effort. Metchie and Young already have a connection from their time at Alabama.
Etienne hasn't seen the field much lately as Hubbard is the Panthers' clear No. 1 back, but Etienne could see more playing time against the Ravens. He only played 11 snaps against the Saints compared to Hubbard's 59.
Etienne is a different kind of runner than Hubbard and gives the Panthers more options on offense. This is especially true as the Panthers try to keep Hubbard fresh for the rest of the season.
The Ravens' run defense is another matchup Carolina needs to respect. Baltimore held the Chargers to just 16 rushing yards in its last game, despite Los Angeles winning 23-20. With defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike out for Sunday's game, Carolina will have a chance to see how its offensive line handles a different defensive front. Giving Etienne a few more carries would also keep Hubbard from having to handle such a heavy workload. Etienne's role in Carolina's backfield has been worth watching.
The Panthers are in for a big game against the Ravens on Sunday. Getting more players involved on offense would be a good thing for this team. Legette, Metchie and Etienne are all players who could be of use to the Panthers on offense and should be given more of an opportunity to play on Sunday.

He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: A Panthers Secret Weapon Is Driving Ridiculous Offensive Success
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers have another weapon on offense in the passing game who is not getting the attention he deserves. While Bryce Young has many targets on the team, tight end Tommy Tremble is the player who gets open the most on the team.
According to Pro Football Focus, Tremble is the only player remaining in the NFL with a 100% separation rate on qualifying targets. In total, Tremble has gotten open on 30 of his 30 targets this year (excluding screen passes). Young has used Tremble as his first read on 66.7% of the tight end's targets.
This is a good sign for the Carolina Panthers' offense. While Tremble may not be leading the Panthers in receiving every week, he is giving Young another reliable option to throw to on offense. It is clear that Young has a lot of faith in Tremble as well.
Tremble has quietly put up some solid numbers this year for Carolina. Through nine games this season, Tremble has caught 25 passes for 227 yards and three touchdowns. In Carolina's last two games, Tremble has caught four passes for 24 yards with a touchdown against Denver, and another four passes for 48 yards against New Orleans.
When you take a look at the PFF numbers for Tremble, it's even more impressive. Not only is he getting open on a high percentage of his targets, but he is the first read for Young on the majority of those targets. This means that the Panthers' coaching staff trusts Tremble to get open and that Young trusts him as well. This is another reliable option for Young to throw to, particularly underneath, that can help keep the offense moving and avoid having to force throws downfield.
For the Carolina offense to be consistent, the Panthers must find more ways to get Tremble involved in the passing game. He is a reliable option underneath and helps create space for other receivers on the offense. Carolina's renewed emphasis on the tight end position makes Tremble's production especially worth watching.
The Panthers will look to build on their recent victory against the New Orleans Saints when they host the Baltimore Ravens in Charlotte, North Carolina. Carolina will try to find ways to keep moving the ball down the field, and Tremble can be a big part of that.
The Ravens will be focused on Carolina's receivers, so Young can look for Tremble underneath. These types of plays may not make the highlight reel, but they can keep drives alive and put the Panthers in better positions on third down.
As the Panthers continue to look for ways to improve on offense, they can expand the role of the tight end and the connection between the quarterback and the player who can get open consistently. Young's recent passing struggles make finding dependable options even more important.
Tremble is obviously not the first option for the Panthers on offense, but the numbers that PFF is looking at for Tremble show that Carolina should be paying more attention to him as the Panthers try to build on their recent win.
