title: Grand Theft Draft Pick: Packers’ Biggest Steals Since Last Grand Theft Auto
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – This week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest entertainment launch in history. It’s estimated it could cost U.S. businesses $1 billion in lost productivity.
Considering the nature of the game, that got us to thinking about the biggest draft steals for the Green Bay Packers, and where they’ve made a killing since GTA V debuted in September 2013. So, here is Grand Theft Draft spanning the release dates.
Talk about being thrown into a pressure cooker. The Packers – fresh off a trip to the NFC Championship Game – traded up in the first round of the 2020 draft to select quarterback Jordan Love at No. 26 overall. The task? Eventually replace Hall of Famer-in-waiting Aaron Rodgers, who replaced Hall of Famer Brett Favre.
Love was the fourth quarterback selected behind No. 1 overall pick Joe Burrow, No. 5 pick Tua Tagovailoa and No. 6 pick Justin Herbert. Love’s 96.8 passer rating trails only Burrow (102.9) in the draft class.
Drafting a quarterback is a crapshoot, regardless of the circumstances, but especially so once you get beyond the top prospects.
Over the last decade, 57 quarterbacks have been selected outside the Top 12 of the draft and started at least one game. Love’s 96.8 passer rating trails only Brock Purdy, Lamar Jackson and Dak Prescott. The league median is 78.4. And that’s just the quarterbacks who were good enough to start.
Quarterbacks taken in the proximity of Love’s spot at No. 26 are few and far between. Over the last two decades, only 23 quarterbacks taken between No. 15 and No. 40 threw even one pass, with Love trailing only Jackson in passer rating. The league median from that group is 82.7.
Davante Adams is one of the greatest receivers in NFL history. The 53rd pick of the 2014 draft and the ninth receiver off the board, Adams is a six-time Pro Bowler. Among all receivers drafted in the second round in NFL history, Adams ranks second with 1,047 receptions, fourth with 13,113 yards and first with 121 touchdowns. Adams needs only 30 receptions to pass Anquan Boldin and he’s 30 touchdowns ahead of everyone else.
Adams ranks 14th in NFL history in receptions and sixth in receiving touchdowns. The Packers no doubt will be thrilled to see Adams in street clothes on Thanksgiving Eve against the Rams.
Tucker Kraft practically wins this by default.
Starting with the 2014 draft, the GTA-window third-round picks by the Packers were tight end Richard Rodgers and defensive tackle Khryi Thornton in 2014, receiver-turned-running back Ty Montgomery in 2015, outside linebacker Kyler Fackrell in 2016, defensive tackle Montravius Adams in 2017, linebacker Oren Burks in 2018, tight end Jace Sternberger in 2019, tight end Josiah Deguara in 2020, receiver Amari Rodgers in 2021, lineman Sean Rhyan in 2022, Kraft in 2023, linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper and running back MarShawn Lloyd in 2024, receiver Savion Williams in 2025  and defensive tackle Chris McClellan in 2026.
That’s one bust after another after another, a run of ineptitude interrupted only by some occasional mediocrity.
Kraft emerged as one of the best tight ends in the NFL before last year’s torn ACL. The hope organizationally – especially given Kraft’s contact extension – is he will turn to that elite level.
David Bakhtiari is the steal of steals among fourth-round picks. Bakhtiari, who might have been a Hall of Famer if not for the knee injury that ruined his career and sank the Packers’ Super Bowl hopes in 2020, was drafted in 2013 but a handful of months before the release of GTA 5 .
So, focusing on the window between release dates, we’ll go with safety Evan Williams ahead of a strong list that includes 2022 picks Zack Bako Bewele and Romeo Doubs.
Williams, the 111th pick in 2024, has emerged as not just one of the best young safeties in the NFL but one of the best safeties, period. Williams has 78 tackles, three interceptions and eight passes defensed this season. No other defensive back with 60-plus tackles has more than one interception.
From the 2024 draft class, Williams leads all Day 3 draft picks with seven interceptions and 233 tackles. In the entire draft class, he’s first among defensive backs in tackles and tied for third in interceptions.
“Evan’s a football player. Evan’s a real football player,” secondary coach and defensive pass-game coordinator Bobby Babich said. “Anytime you have that combined with the football mind and that intelligence, usually the product that they’re going to put out there. As long as they care about the game as much as you think they do, that product’s going to be one that everybody likes to watch.”
This was a two-man battle between center Corey Linsley in 2014 and running back Aaron Jones in 2017. We’ll go with Jones because of his longevity.
From the 2017 draft class, Jones leads the way with 8,147 rushing yards, just ahead of Christian McCaffrey (8,108). Since entering the NFL, he trails only 2018 first-round pick Saquan Barkley (8,652) and 2020 second-round pick Jonathan Taylor (8,358).
Jones played with the Packers through 2023. He ranks second in franchise history with 5,940 rushing yards, behind only Ahman Green and Hall of Famer Jim Taylor, and first among running backs with a 5.0-yard average.
There have been no standouts drafted in the sixth round by the Packers since kicker Mason Crosby in 2007. The Packers drafted Isaiah McDuffie with the 220th pick in 2021 and gained a solid, reliable contributor. He ranks 10th in the draft class with 383 tackles; the nine players ahead of him were all top-125 picks. He has at least 109 tackles more than every player drafted after him.
“He’s a pro’s pro,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said last week. “He’s awesome throughout the week. He’s awesome on gameday. He gives really good insight when we come off [the field] what’s going on, what he’s seeing, the communication piece of all that. And he’s made a lot of plays. Playing well.”
The Packers were more than happy to let Rasheed Walker go in free agency this offseason, but he was a Godsend after David Bakhtiari’s career was ruined by a knee injury.
At a position group filled mostly by first-round picks around the league, Walker was the 249th out of 262 players drafted in 2022. He started 48 games as Jordan Love’s blind-side protector from 2023 through 2025. He had a lot more good snaps than bad.
The Packers drafted 22 players in the seventh round from 2014 through 2026. Walker and cornerback Carrington Valentine were the only starters. In fact, you’ve got to go back to center Scott Wells (2014) as the only Packers seventh-round pick who was a full-time starter for at least as many seasons as Walker.

title: Packers Report Card at Bye Week: One ‘A’ In Our Unit Grades on Defense
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers will take a 6-4 record out of their bye week and into a Thanksgiving Eve showdown at the Rams.
Jonathan Gannon’s defense is a mediocre 14th with 22.1 points allowed per game, due in part to the offense’s two horrific performances against the Vikings skewing the bottom line. Only the Vikings and Jaguars (seven apiece) have allowed 20-or-fewer points in more games than the Packers (six). They rank 11th in total defense but second in takeaways, fourth in sacks and fourth in passes defensed.
With the table set, here is a Packers midseason report card on defense.
This position, of course, was the major question mark entering the season. How would Green Bay’s defense survive the first four or six games without Micah Parsons? Well, as it turns out, the defense has survived 10 games without Parsons.
The Packers flipped the switch on Lukas Van Ness’s fifth-year option, a $13.752 million gamble on a player who had a total of 8.5 sacks in his first three seasons. Through 10 games this season, he has six sacks. That gives him a decent chance of getting to at least 10 sacks – a significant milestone for a pass rusher.
Fellow starter Barryn Sorrell has two sacks. The backups, Brenton Cox and Dani Dennis-Sutton, have been productive. Cox has only 1.5 sacks but is second on the team with eight quarterback hits. Dennis-Sutton, a fourth-round rookie, is tied for second on the team with three sacks and is third with seven quarterback hits.
Those four each have 159 pass-rushing snaps, a threshold met by 70 edge rushers. Van Ness ranks eighth in pass-rush win rate and 11th pass-rush productivity, a PFF metric that encompasses sacks, hits and hurries per pass-rushing snap. Sorrell is 44th in win rate and 59th in PRP, Cox is 23rd in win rate and 18th in PRP, and Dennis-Sutton is 50th in win rate and 16th in PRP.
Something that doesn’t show up in the stat is their edge-setting ability, and they’ve done well in that regard.
“That was a question that was routinely asked throughout camp is how is this edge group going to be able to perform without Micah,” Van Ness said last week.” I think we were all very aware that we’d have to pick up our end of the bargain until Micah returned. I’m proud of the way we’ve done that.
“I feel like from Day 1, we just attacked camp – from OTAs to camp to all the way throughout the season – and I think you’ve seen that production week after week after week. I’m proud of the way we’re trending. Just got to keep it going.”
Green Bay’s defensive tackles have contributed little statistically but are an unsung reason for the team’s overall success.
Led by Karl Brooks, who has three sacks and six tackles for losses, the defensive tackles have contributed 7.5 sacks and 12 TFLs, according to the official stats, and 43 pressures, according to PFF. Chicago’s Jeffery Simmons has six sacks and nine TFLs by himself, and Denver’s Zach Allen has 38 pressures.
The defense has been strong, though, whether it’s stopping the run or rushing the passer, and this group is a reason why. The depth has been critical with Javon Hargrave, Jonathan Ford and Warren Brinson on injured reserve.
They’ve been good but they can be better. Brooks has three sacks in the last two games. That’s a good start. Devonte Wyatt, however, has been invisible following last year’s season-ending injury.
To get him off the fifth-year option, the Packers gave Wyatt a three-year, $54.9 million contract extension through 2029. He has three sacks and four TFLs. They’ve been rewarded with nine pressures, which is tied for 76th among defensive tackles.
“His juice, his energy on the field, off the field is very contagious and is electric,” position coach Vince Oghobaase said in defending Wyatt this week. “I do know D-Wy is a very prideful guy who wants to be great. He’ll work his tail off and he’s been doing that.
“Sometimes the impact guys have interior-wise is not always going to be seen on the stat sheet and I’m aware of that and he’s aware of that. Obviously, we all want the stats – the sacks, the TFLs and all the tackles but that’s not always how the game shakes out. As long as you are impacting the game, you are doing your job.”
During training camp, it was clear that the Packers’ best top-to-bottom position group was the linebacker corps. That’s exactly how it’s played out – and it’s saved the team’s season.
With Edgerrin Cooper out for the season with a torn Achilles and Zaire Franklin missing four games with an injured shin, Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper have come to the rescue. And when one of them has been banged up, Nick Niemann has provided solid snaps.
McDuffie leads the group with 56 tackles, including one sack and three for losses. Franklin has 41 tackles, including two for losses. Hopper has 26 tackles but has two interceptions and ranks sixth on the team with six pass breakups. Cooper still is tied for second on the team with three sacks and six tackles for losses.
They have tackled at a high level, played with physicality and carried out the plan, regardless of who’s in there.
“I think resiliency, obviously, is the first word that comes to mind,” linebackers coach Sam Siefkes said. “You mentioned the next man up, it’s kind of been the epitome of that I think for the majority of this season. It’s just next guy be ready to play no matter when it is, and we’ve had a lot of guys that have had to step up and I think have done a nice job playing in those roles.”
If grading on a curve because of circumstances, this would be an A. But, for the bottom line …
If there was one reason to doubt the Packers heading into training camp, it was the cornerback group’s ability to hold up without an elite pass rush. In 2025, Keisean Nixon ranked fifth in touchdowns allowed (seven) and first in penalties (12), Carrington Valentine was benched a couple times because of his horrendous tackling and Brandon Cisse was at South Carolina.
What a difference a coaching staff makes, apparently.
Nixon was challenged during training camp and responded. He’s allowed one touchdown and been guilty of three penalties. Cisse, a second-round pick, might be the best rookie corner in the league. Valentine lost the starting job to Cisse but has played well off the bench – including as a tackler.
“On gameday, he’s one of the most locked in as far as what’s happening in the game that I’ve ever been around,” secondary coach and defensive pass-game coordinator Bobby Babich said of Nixon. “He’s a football guy. He loves the game of football, which is where it all starts.”
Cisse has one interception and nine passes defensed. His seven-game streak without allowing a touchdown ended on the play in which he was injured against Minnesota. Nixon has one interception and eight passes defensed. He’s allowing just 9.0 yards per catch. In limited action, Valentine is allowing 8.0 yards per catch and looks like a new player with his physicality and tackling.
Overall, Green Bay has allowed the fifth-fewest completions of 25-plus yards. They are fourth in yards allowed per attempt and fifth in yards allowed per completion. The one knock might be that Cisse and Nixon have missed too many tackles, but the mentality has been there.
“One thing that stands out is the love they have for one another,” position coach Daniel Bullocks said. “Obviously, it’s a talented group, but the love that they have for one another, the respect they have for one another, what they demand from one another.
“The great defensive backs rooms that I’ve been a part of, there’s three things that’s in common. Guys eliminate explosive plays; they do a great job of that. And taking the ball away, No. 2, another thing they do a good job there. And also they tackle. Those guys love football and you talk about our play-style, they represent all of that.”
Everybody knew this was the team’s best unit, but maybe even they’ve surpassed expectations. Xavier McKinney has an NFL-leading six interceptions and Evan Williams has three.…

title: Packers Report Card at Bye Week: One ‘F’ In Our Unit Grades on Offense
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are 6-4 at the bye and will face a make-or-break seven-game dash either toward the playoffs or over a cliff.
To reach the postseason, the Packers must become much more efficient on offense. They rank a modest 13th with 22.6 points per game due in large part to ranking 32nd in rushing, 19th on third down and 21st in the red zone.
Here’s a bye-week report card on offense.
Jordan Love has had to carry the offense to a greater extent than Aaron Rodgers was ever asked to during his legendary career. The Packers’ 67.0 rushing yards per game is just a half-yard better than the Chargers’ all-time worst of 66.4 rushing yards per game in 2000.
The offensive line has been bad. The running backs have been ineffective. And the receivers have treated his passes like the balls are made of a combination of molten lava and radioactive waste.
Of 31 quarterbacks to have thrown 140 passes, Love has been plagued by the most drops (25) and the second-highest drop rate (9.7 percent), according to Pro Football Focus.
What a completely different game Love has had to play compared to his peers. Brock Purdy, the quarterback of the NFC-leading 49ers, has had five passes dropped. Jared Goff, the quarterback of the NFC North-leading Lions, has had six passes dropped. Caleb Williams, the quarterback of the Bears, has had seven passes dropped. That’s a combined 18 passes dropped – nowhere near what Love has endured.
And yet the Packers are 6-4 despite the two-fold pressure of what defenses have thrown at him and what he’s had to do to keep the whole thing from sinking.
About the only knock on him is he needs to get better at taking some of the layups that defenses are giving him.
Josh Jacobs missed the first six games on the exempt list and then most of one game and all of another with a broken finger. Of the team’s 10 games, he’s played less than 100 snaps.
Jacobs has carried 36 times for 80 yards, or a meager 2.2-yard average. It’s obviously a small sample size, but Jacobs in 2024 rushed for 1,329 yards, averaged 4.4 yards per carry, had a success rate of 52.2 percent and averaged 2.4 yards after contact, according to Stathead.
Jacobs’ rushing average is exactly half of what he gained in 2024, his success rate has crashed to 38.9 percent and he’s averaging 1.0 yards after contact. He is sixth on the team with 11 catches, which is rather remarkable given his limited playing time.
Kaleb Johnson spent about half the season in the doghouse after a couple fumbles but has a team-high 214 rushing yards with a 4.1-yard average. MarShawn Lloyd, who the Packers waited on following two injury-ruined seasons, has 162 rushing yards with a 2.7-yard average. Chris Brooks returned from injured reserve last week. He has 71 rushing yards and a 4.2 average.
Ultimately, good running backs get what’s blocked and then get more. Added together, according to Stathead, the Packers are 30th with 1.4 yards after contact per carry. They’re a middle-of-the-pack 21.9 rushing attempts per missed tackle, which shows just how awful the blocking has been in that there’s been no reward for making defenders miss.
Of the 74 backs with at least 25 carries, Johnson is fifth in yards after contact per carry. The others? Pierre Strong is 68th, Jacobs is 71st and Lloyd is 72nd.
Christian Watson is third with 916 receiving yards and Matthew Golden is fifth with 853 receiving yards. Their 1,769 receiving yards are No. 1 among duos, just ahead of the 1,702 yards by Cincinnati’s Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins They have combined for 62.3 percent of the team passing yards, behind only the combined 63.5 percent by Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Cooper Kupp.
Watson has been tremendous. The Packers haven’t had a 1,000-yard receiver since 2021; he’s on pace to blow past 1,500 yards.
Watson has dropped three passes and is 14-of-21 in contested-catch situations. Of 47 receivers who have been targeted at least 40 times, he is third in yards per route (2.80), 24th in drop percentage (5.5) and tied for eighth in contested-catch percentage (66.7). Plus, he is third with 10 receptions on passes thrown 20-plus yards downfield.
Golden’s numbers are great, too, but a lot of that is a byproduct of volume. He is third in the league with 101 targets. Of the 47 receivers who have been targeted at least 40 times, he is 42nd in catch percentage (58.6), 12th in yards per route (2.42), last in drop percentage (15.9) and 38th in contested-catch percentage (38.9). His 11 drops, using PFF’s numbers, are five more than any other receiver.
While he is fifth in deep receptions with nine, his 27 deep targets are six more than any other player.
In five games since coming off injured reserve, Savion Williams has caught 13-of-15 passes for 136 yards. Aside from J. Michael Sturdivant’s touchdown vs. Minnesota, nobody else has made a play that’s mattered.
In eight games last season, Tucker Kraft caught 32 passes for 489 yards and six touchdowns. In 10 games in his comeback season, Kraft has caught 37 passes for 370 yards (10.0 average) and three touchdowns.
Using PFF’s numbers, his yards per target are down from 11.1 to 6.6, his YAC per catch has been cut almost in half from 10.8 to 5.5 and his yards per route has been sliced from 2.22 to 1.29. Of 33 tight ends who have been targeted at least 28 times, Kraft is 23rd in yards per route, 13th in YAC per catch and 31st in drop percentage (9.8).
“I don’t want to answer any more questions about numbers,” he said after several questions following a one-catch game against New England, which he followed up with a one-catch game against Minnesota. “I want you guys to know I don’t care about any of that. So, that’s always been my standard. I put the team first every time. I don’t want to talk about stats anymore or fantasy or anything like that.”
ACL injuries are a challenge to come back from, and the challenge has been ratcheted up by the poor play of the offensive line.
Mark Redman has been a considerable contributor as a run blocker. Jonnu Smith hasn’t been given hardly any opportunities in the passing game, Josh Whyle is on injured reserve and Luke Musgrave hasn’t played.
This unit, of course, has been the root of most of the team’s problems.
Including right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, who suffered a season-ending knee injury during the second game of the season, they’ve had 10 players play at least 71 snaps. There have been six starting combinations. There have been four starting left guards and three starting right guards. Laken Tomlinson went from Dallas’ practice squad to starting four games at left guard, two games at right guard and then one more back at left guard. Travis Glover went from injured to starting to injured to starting. The team’s No. 3 center, John Williams, has started three games. That’s as many starts as the team’s $77 million left guard, Aaron Banks, who was benched for the Minnesota game.
“I think the biggest thing is just we’ve just got to keep coaching them,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “We’ve just got to keep believing in each other and we’ve just got to keep fighting. There’s going to be setbacks, but the one thing is you can’t let the setback make you worse after that. It’s got to make you better. We’ve got to take a step forward from here.
“As far as who’s in, who’s playing, again, the injury situation, we still don’t know that. We’ve just got to roll with the punches and figure it out, and just keep doing what we’ve been trying to do with putting the best five out there that we feel is going to give us a chance to win the game. That’s going to be one thing we’ve got to do when we evaluate this as the week unfolds.”
Using PFF’s pass-blocking efficiency metric, which takes sacks, hits and hurries allowed per pass-blocking snap, there have been 62 tackles who have played at least 200 pass-blocking snaps. title: Packers Create Roster Spot, And That Means Two Things
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers on Thursday announced they released running back Pierre Strong.
That leaves the Packers with a 52-man roster. You know what that means.
All signs point to Micah Parsons making his debut against the Rams on Wednesday. Before he can take aim at Los Angeles quarterback Matthew Stafford, he’ll need to be added to the 53-man roster. The release of Strong made that possible.
“First of all, I just want to praise him for his work and our training staff for all the things they’ve been doing to get back to be ready to perform for our football team,” position coach DeMarcus Covington said this week. “And it’s been fun working with him. Obviously, worked with him last year and as he’s been getting ready to play, whenever that is, him being in the classroom, he’s always been in the classroom with us the whole time.
“And he’s done a really good job with that leadership portion, helping us out throughout the week, film study with the guys and then also just giving his evaluation within the meeting room. And then also you guys see him on the sideline, he’s been doing a really good job stepping up as far as his leadership role during the time that he’s not on the field. He’s been doing a good job in the classroom with our guys, too. Excited to eventually get him out there so he can help our defense, help our team win some football games.”
The release of Pierre Strong leaves the Packers with four running backs on their roster: Josh Jacobs, Kaleb Johnson, Chris Brooks and MarShawn Lloyd.
The Packers had five running backs on their roster. In the loss to the Vikings, Jacobs was out with a broken finger and Strong was a healthy scratch. By snaps, Brooks led the way with 26 in his return from injured reserve, followed by 14 apiece from Johnson and Lloyd. By touches, Johnson had 10 (all rushes), Lloyd had seven (four rushes, three catches) and Brooks had three (two rushes, one catch).
Jacobs had surgery to repair his broken right ring finger. It was a clean break, meaning a quick return to the lineup. Could that be against the Rams? After a mini-bye, the Packers will return to the practice field on Saturday.
Whether Jacobs returns this week or next week, the release of Strong clearly means the team does not believe Jacobs will be out much longer.
Once everyone is healthy, it’ll be interesting to see which direction the Packers turn in the backfield. Jacobs is the proven workhorse who they’ve waited for through thick and thin this year. Johnson has been the most impactful runner. Brooks has a critical role as a trusted pass protector. Lloyd is the former third-round pick.
Johnson would seem to have a role going forward based on how he played against Minnesota.
“There were some flashes, obviously,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “There were some good runs in there. But the one thing about Kaleb is you can feel him attack the line of scrimmage. He was coming off the ball really well. He was running hard. So that was really encouraging, to see him go out there and do that. I’m very excited about him as we move forward, for sure.”
The Packers have a total of 11 players on injured lists. Of those, only Micah Parsons has been designated for return.
Four are out for the season: right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (Achilles), defensive tackle Javon Hargrave (Achilles) and receiver Jayden Reed (neck).
The others, in terms of their return to game action:
Defensive tackle Warren Brinson’s groin injury required surgery. Asked about him last week, coach Matt LaFleur said: “it usually takes a little bit longer time to recover than five weeks.” After a significant injury, he’d obviously need some ramp-up to get him on the field.
Defensive tackle Jonathan Ford was placed on injured reserve on Oct. 17 with a calf injury. He is eligible to be designated to return.
Center/guard Jacob Monk replaced Sean Rhyan in the Detroit game on Oct. 25 but suffered a quad injury. He was placed on injured reserve the next day and has to spend at least one more week on IR before he can return to practice.
Tight end Josh Whyle was placed on injured reserve last week with a concussion so will be out at least three more games.
Edge Collin Oliver was placed on injured reserve at the end of training camp, presumably due to the calf injury he sustained in the second preseason game at Denver. When Parsons spoke to reporters a couple weeks ago, he mentioned Oliver had a “setback” in his recovery.
Tight end Luke Musgrave is on PUP with the neck injury sustained during the offseason. Obviously, the longer Musgrave is out, the more unlikely it is that he will return this season.
Of note, teams can bring back eight players from injured reserve during the regular season. Savion Williams and Oliver (who were designated to return at the end of camp) along with Chris Brooks and Skyy Moore mean the Packers have used four. Parsons, because he opened training camp on PUP, does not count against the eight.

title: Good News, Bad News, Projections From Packers’ Long List of 2027 Free Agents
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The NFL Draft is the lifeblood of the Green Bay Packers. While general manager Brian Gutekunst has been more aggressive in free agency and trades and less reluctant to find veterans for in-season help, the draft remains the team’s primary source of talent.
After this season, the 2023 NFL Draft class is scheduled to reach free agency. First-round pick Lukas Van Ness was given the fifth-year option, so he’ll be back for 2027, and second-round receiver Jayden Reed and third-round tight end Tucker Kraft earned contract extensions. However, of the team’s other 10 draft picks, seven are no longer on the team and only one is a starter.
A dud of a draft class is the bad news. The good news is there shouldn’t be much stress on Gutekunst or the salary cap in terms of determining who to keep and who to let go.
With that as a backdrop, here are the Packers’ 16 unrestricted free agents, listed in order of playing time on offense and defense, according to OverTheCap.com, plus a prediction on whether they will stay or go.
Nixon, who will turn 30 in June, picked a fine time to play the best football of his career in terms of his work on defense. Nixon allowed seven touchdowns and was penalized 12 times last season. This season, he has allowed one touchdown and been penalized three times. While he’s on pace to allow a career-high 66 completions, according to Pro Football Focus, most of them have been short catches.
The Packers typically don’t re-sign 30-year-olds, and that probably will remain true even though he’s as tough as a $2 steak, but he’s set himself up for a nice payday.
Projection: Will not return because of age and the team’s salary cap.
After the Week 3 debacle against Atlanta, the Packers grabbed the 34-year-old Tomlinson off Dallas’ practice squad. He’s played almost every snap in seven starts, bouncing from four starts at left guard to two at right guard and now one back at left guard.
PFF has charged him with only one sack. He hasn’t been great, obviously, but he’s been a phenomenal bargain compared to Aaron Banks .
Projection: Will not return.
Of the upcoming free agents who were drafted in 2023, Brooks is the only starter. The former sixth-round pick is having a fantastic season. After recording just a half-sack and one tackle for loss in 16 games (seven starts) last season, Brooks has three sacks and six tackles for losses in 10 games (all starts) this year. He leads the unit with 14 pressures.
“I thought he played probably his best game since I’ve been here in my mind and he lit it up vs. New England, too,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said this week. “From a play-style standpoint, always on point. Schematic and technical executions, most of the time is on point.
“He’s a guy that plays a lot of different spots. To the eye just watching the game, plays defensive tackle. Yes, he does. But we align him in a lot of different spots by front structure, by who we have out there, and I feel good about him doing everything.”
Nixon, Tomlinson and Brooks are the only free agents playing more than half the snaps. Brooks routinely plays the most snaps of the defensive tackles.
Projection: Will not return because he’s playing his way out of Green Bay’s price range.
The former undrafted free agent has only 1.5 sacks but he’s second on the team with eight quarterback hits (official stats) and 26 pressures (PFF). Of 72 edge rushers with at least 150 pass-rushing opportunities, Cox is tied for 23rd in PFF’s pass-rush win rate, which is just behind Will Anderson and just ahead of Trey Hendrickson and Danielle Hunter.
Cox has played 40.5 percent of the snaps; the return of Micah Parsons will cut into it but perhaps not by much.
The Packers signed Smith at the end of training camp. It seemed like a brilliant signing considering he caught 50 passes for the Falcons in 2023, 88 passes for the Dolphins in 2024 and 38 passes for the Steelers in 2025. In nine games for the Packers, though, he has only six receptions, including just one in the team’s last six games.
Projection: Will not return.
The addition of Brandon Cisse in this year’s draft cost Valentine his starting job. A seventh-round pick in 2023, he came off the bench against the Vikings and had one of his better games. He’s always been able to cover; he’s allowed just 88 yards on 17 targets this season, according to PFF. What was noteworthy, given his career-long ineptitude as a tackler, was his physicality against the run and a couple receiver screens.
“I would say this: When we got here, everyone had a clean slate, want-to and physicality was not his issue when we got here,” defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said. “It was technique. I think he’s worked really hard on that with DB [Daniel Bullocks] and Bobby [Babich] of cleaning up some technique. If you have the wrong technique, it can look to the naked eye as one thing but it’s really not that. He is not soft, he is not afraid at all. He just had to clean up his technique. I thought he came in and played extremely well.”
Projection: Could return if the price is right, because the Packers will need a starter opposite Cisse in 2027.
A seventh-round pick in 2022 who never played in a game during his first go-around with the team, Ford returned late last season and earned a roster spot this season. He’s played in five games (one start) but missed the last five games due to injury. A big run-stopping force, he had the first half-sack of his career in Week 1.
Strong, a fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022, spent last year on Green Bay’s practice squad. This season, he’s played in five games, carried 25 times for 59 yards (2.4 average) and caught 10 passes for 61 yards (6.1 average). He might be the odd man out on the roster once Josh Jacobs returns.
Moore returned from injured reserve following an ankle injury, only to suffer another ankle injury on his third kickoff return against Minnesota. He leads the team with a 27.2-yard average on kickoff returns and a 14.8-yard average on punt returns but has been a nonfactor with his 93 snaps on offense.
He’s got a chance to be ready to face the Rams.
Projection: Will return if he can get on the field and stay on the field.
Niemann is perhaps the team’s best player on special teams. He ranks first on the team in snaps (208) and second in tackles (nine), and he played well while playing most of the game at linebacker against New England.
Whyle, who caught 28 passes for the Titans in 2024, was part of the Packers replacing Tucker Kraft last season. After catching five passes in eight games in 2025, he has zero catches in eight games in 2026 and is on injured reserve following a concussion.
Projection: Will not return.
Once again, Welch fell short of a spot on Green Bay’s roster at the end of training camp. Once again, Welch is a key player on special teams. He is sixth on the team in snaps and has six tackles.
With quarterbacks dropping like flies around the league, Taylor has only had to play mop-up duty for the Packers. The 37-year-old who was signed to replace Malik Willis is with the team because of his experience, knowhow and ability to help Jordan Love behind the scenes.
Projection: Will not return.
The Packers signed Becton to the practice squad following the Week 3 debacle. A first-round bust as a left tackle, he resurrected his career as a right guard for the Eagles in 2024 and Chargers in 2025. He’s played 11 snaps on offense in two games. That includes three as an extra tight end against Minnesota, and those didn’t go well with one sack and one additional pressure allowed.
Projection: Will return as an inexpensive bridge player following the potential departures of Aaron Banks, Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler.
A second-round pick in 2023, Musgrave should be in the prime of his career. Instead, his career has fallen off a cliff following a promising rookie season. He has not been on the practice field since June due to a neck injury.
Projection: Will not return.

title: Grand Theft Contract: Six Worst Packers Free-Agent Signings of GTA Era
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Today’s the day some gamers have been waiting for for years. It’s the release date for Grand Theft Auto VI .
That got us thinking about the six worst free-agent signings in Green Bay Packers history, or at least since the original GTA debuted in 1997. Here are our picks, in order from bad to worst.
Jeff Saturday was a five-time Pro Bowler and two-time All-Pro while with the Colts. After 13 excellent seasons alongside Peyton Manning, he joined the Packers in 2012 on a two-year, $7.75 million contract. Saturday was signed to replace standout Scott Wells but was benched late in his debut season and retired after the season.
At least there was no signing bonus involved, so the Packers were able to wash their hands of the situation.
The Packers under first-year general manager Brian Gutekunst took a big swing at a chronic problem by signing five-time Pro Bowl tight end Jimmy Graham to a three-year, $30 million contract in 2018. To create space for Graham’s top-of-the-market contract, which included $11 million guaranteed, the Packers released fan-favorite but past-his-prime Jordy Nelson.
Graham wasn’t terrible. Far from it. He just wasn’t the player who caught 10 touchdown passes in 2017 or had four seasons of more than 900 yards. He caught 55 passes for 636 yards and two touchdowns in 2018 and 38 passes for 447 yards and three touchdowns in 2019. The Packers released him in March 2020.
In 2016, tight end Jared Cook was one of the key players for an injury-plagued team that reached the NFC Championship Game. The Packers were unable to re-sign Cook, so pivoted to Martellus Bennett. His three-year, $21 million contract included a $6.3 million signing bonus.
He played just seven games for the Packers before an ugly divorce in which he accused the Packers’ conservative medical staff of making him play through a shoulder injury.
Bennett signed with the Packers due in part to the presence of Aaron Rodgers. Did Rodgers’ broken collarbone affect Bennett’s shoulder?
“You can’t deny the facts of your timeline and how everything went down,” then-coach Mike McCarthy said. “Really, to tie all that together, you’re asking me to get inside somebody else’s feelings, conversation, more on a personal level. I think this all started coming out of the bye week. Everything leading up to that, I can’t really comment on it. And then we went down this injury path and then here we are today.”
Not all contracts are created equally.
In free agency in 2024, Gutekunst signed running back Josh Jacobs to a four-year, $48 million contract that included a $12.5 million signing bonus and got a centerpiece of the offense. In 2025, Gutekunst signed Hobbs to a four-year, $48 million contract that included a $16 million signing bonus. The $12 million averaged ranked 21st among cornerbacks.
“We just really thought he’s a really versatile all-around corner, can do everything,” Gutekunst said at the time. “We really like his ability to play on the outside, which he hasn’t done a ton of, but the ability to move him inside and match different receivers, and his play style I think is one of the things that really stood out to all of us. Really, really excited to see what he’s going to do for us this year.”
Instead of a centerpiece of the defense, the Packers dumped him overboard after one season with an equal mix of injuries and ineffective play. Hobbs played 32 percent of the defensive snaps. PFF charged him with a 125.3 passer rating when targeted. He gave up two touchdowns and broke up two passes.
It’s a mystery why the signing didn’t work out . In four years with the Raiders, he missed 17 games due to injuries, started 38 games and intercepted three passes. The Packers projected Hobbs as an every-down player, though there was little evidence of him being that type of player.
The Packers ate $4 million of dead cap for this season and will ingest another $8 million next season.
After sitting out the 1999 season due to a knee injury, Johnson was named the NFL’s Comeback Player of the Year in 2000 with his 12 sacks. After adding another nine sacks in 2021, the Packers in 2002 under then-general manager Mike Sherman signed Johnson away from the Saints with a six-year contract worth $33 million that included a $6.5 million signing bonus.
Johnson had two sacks in five games in 2002 and zero sacks in six games in 2023. The Packers got rid of him after that season, and he never played in another NFL game.
“We watched him on tape and he looked great and did a lot of good things,” Sherman said. “It’s unfortunate that he’s had the injuries that he’s had. I think everybody learns lessons from everything they do in this business or any business.”
Gutekunst had impeccable forays into free agency in 2019 and 2024 but whiffed on Banks and Hobbs in 2025.
Banks signed a four-year, $77 million contract. The $19.25 million average ranks ninth among guards. The signing came as an incredible overreaction to the Packers getting overwhelmed physically in the 2024 playoff loss at the Eagles.
Banks had been a solid but not spectacular starter for the 49ers; the Packers gave great-player money to a player who had never been great.
Coaches like to say a player’s greatest ability is his availability. After playing only five offensive snaps as a rookie second-round pick by the 49ers in 2021, Banks played 88.3 percent of the snaps in 2022, 78.5 percent in 2023 and 71.8 percent in 2024. With Green Bay, he has been dogged by a mountain of lower-body injuries.
After starting against Carolina and New England, Banks was on the bench against Minnesota. The Packers opted to start Laken Tomlinson, who was signed off Dallas’ practice squad, at left guard and Travis Glover, who had missed the past two games with a knee injury, at right guard. Ten games into the season, Banks has played 70 percent of the snaps in only one game. He might be the No. 4 guard behind Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Glover against the Rams after the bye.
“I think the biggest thing is just the consistency aspect, getting him out there – his health, obviously, is huge,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said this week “And I think just getting him out there playing with consistency, it’s going to be the biggest thing.”
The Packers’ offensive line is a mess. Signing Banks and moving on from Elgton Jenkins is a big reason why.
Banks is owed a $9.5 million roster bonus at the start of the league-year in March. There is almost a 0 percent chance that will be paid and the worst contract in NFL history will be off the roster (if not off the financial ledger, with a residual dead-cap charge of about $26.3 million).
Typically, I'm a glass-half-empty kind of person. Today, let me bring some sunshine to a cloudy day. Yeah, the Packers got trounced on Sunday, but I've got six reasons why they can (and will) rebound. ⬇️ https://t.co/YPVQLYyTHn

title: Packers Bye Week Rookie Report Card: It’s Been a Snap for Draft Picks
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst faced a draft with great challenges but great importance.
The challenge? The Packers didn’t have a first-round pick because of the Micah Parsons trade and had only one compensatory pick. The importance? Gutekunst had built a top-heavy roster, so there was a need for young, low-cost talent to come in and fill holes.
The Packers wound up with only six draft picks. Three of them have played well in considerable playing time. Here’s a look at the draft class at the bye, with grades done on a curve relative to their draft positioning.
Even while missing most of Sunday’s loss to the Vikings with a rib injury, Brandon Cisse leads all rookie cornerbacks with 573 snaps. He hadn’t given up a touchdown since Week 2 until bouncing off Minnesota’s Myles Price on the play in which he was injured.
“He’s a smart player,” position coach Daniel Bullocks said on Tuesday. “Doesn’t make the same mistake twice. As a defensive back, you got to have a short memory because, JG’s right, you play this game long enough, you going to get beat. He has the resilience to not get beat twice by the same play and that goes with his preparation. That’s a credit to him getting better, working the technique each and every week.”
The JG from that quote is, obviously, defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. Gannon was bullish on Cisse’s potential from the jump, which is why he worked with the No. 1 defense throughout training camp.
What Gannon needed to see was how Cisse would respond to adversity. That first taste came when he gave up a touchdown pass to Justin Jefferson in the opener.
“Remember you guys asked me where can he go, and I said I’ll tell you when I see some balls get caught on him,” Gannon said last week. “Week 1, he got a bomb caught on him and he responded the right way. So, that was huge to me. That was kind of the first measuring stick of when we get into the season how is this guy going to be? He’s got quite a bit of resilience about his game.”
Gannon said resiliency is the key for any cornerback. There is no such thing as a “shutdown cornerback.” Just go back to how the Packers beat up on Christian Gonzalez a couple weeks ago against New England. Even the best corners in the league get beat. Only seven are giving up a catch rate of less than 50 percent.
“You are going to get beat,” Gannon said. “They are going to make plays and they’re going to catch the ball on you. It doesn’t matter how talented, how good you are. I think there’s a mindset and a resiliency, there’s a focus, all that psych, that goes into being a good player, especially with that position.
“When you get back in the huddle, are you saying, you want the ball to come to you again or do you get back in the huddle and you say, ‘Man, I hope the ball doesn’t get thrown at me?’ The great ones I’ve been around want the ball thrown right to them again. So, I think that’s a huge thing.”
Chris McClellan leads all rookie defensive tackles with 315 snaps. He has not made a huge statistical impact with 19 tackles, zero sacks and zero tackles for losses in 10 games, but the Packers aren’t asking their defensive tackles to be game-wreckers.
Position coach Vince Oghobaase said McClellan has done well in playing multiple positions up front while helping the team overcome injuries that sent Javon Hargrave, Jonathan Ford and Warren Brinson to injured reserve.
“One of the hardest things is consistency as a defensive lineman,” Oghobaase said, “especially early on in a young guy’s career like that – taking on the double-teams, preparing a certain way every single week, making sure everything from a scouting standpoint, a rep standpoint, a practice standpoint, that he’s doing the same things over and over again. That way he can perform consistently on Sunday.
“That’s my biggest deal for him is just being consistent because he makes some plays when he’s out there. But sometimes he has those bad plays that kind of stand out and how do we get back from those.”
Dennis-Sutton ranks fourth among rookie edge players with 314 snaps even while being the 120th pick. He has three sacks, four tackles for losses and two passes defensed. According to PFF, he’s third among rookies with 23 pressures; only No. 2 overall pick David Bailey and second-round pick Gabe Jacas have more.
His strong play against the run should keep him on the field once Micah Parsons returns.
“I think his attention to detail in the classroom carries over to the practice field,” position coach DeMarcus Covington said. “His effort makes up for a lot of things where he can just win with effort and not giving up on plays. You see him on special teams running down, you see him trying to block a freakin’ punt. He’s doing whatever we ask him to do at a high level and with no hesitation. And he’s able to line up in different spots.
“So, of course, you’re going to have some rookie mistakes here and there, but he does a really good job playing with high effort, getting out the stack, rushing the passer, setting the edge and all the above. So, I’m excited about his development and where he’s going, trending upwards and as long as we continue to do that, I think he’ll be a find for the Green Bay Packers.”
He already has been a find.
Jager Burton made his first career start against Atlanta in Week 3. His struggles in that game led to the Packers signing Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton in the following days.
“For me, it’s like how can you find a way to turn stuff into positive things, and now I have guys that have been doing it at a really high level for 10 years,” Burton said at the time. “It feels like, if you’re in the business world and you go to a conference and see all these other people and pick their brains. Now we’ve got all these guys here who have been everywhere and so it’s just awesome to get to talk to them.”
Domani Jackson is the only one of Green Bay’s six draft picks who did not make the 53-man roster. He’s spent the season on the practice squad and not gotten into a game.
His development this season will be important with Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine set to be free agents.
Trey Smack missed a 53-yarder against Minnesota on Sunday. Out of 30 kickers who have attempted more than 10 field goals, Smack is 28th in field-goal percentage (71.4) and 27th in extra-point percentage (87.5). He’s missed a league-high nine total kicks.
Special teams coordinator Cam Achord chalked some of it up to “rookie growing pains” on Tuesday. Among the three rookies with more than 10 field-goal attempts, Smack is last in field-goal accuracy and second in extra-point percentage.
“You look at the league right now, I think there’s a couple other rookies that may not be doing great, too,” Achord said. “Some of that is the rookie stuff, and some of it is the consistency of the contact, which I think we can improve. You hope the more you get through the season, like that continues to get better and improve, and you hope you’re on the trend of the upward part of it towards the end, that you’re playing your best football here, December, moving forward.”
Smack was the first kicker drafted this year. Over the last 20 drafts, 13 kickers were drafted in the sixth round and attempted at least one field goal as a rookie. Smack’s 71.4 percent ranks last.

title: With Sky Falling, Here Are Six Reasons Why Packers Can (And Will) Rebound
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were beaten to a pulp by the Minnesota Vikings in every way imaginable on Sunday.
A high-powered passing game that dropped a series of bombs on the Patriots last week bombed against the elite Vikings defense. Green Bay’s defense couldn’t get off the field against a Vikings passing attack that played without three top performers. Green Bay’s special teams were outplayed.
It’s easy to be consumed by the doom and gloom, especially given how coach Matt LaFleur’s team seemed completely unprepared for the challenge. However, the Packers are 6-4 and, in a lot of ways, the arrow is pointed up.
Here are six reasons for optimism heading into the home stretch.
Lost in the shuffle of Green Bay’s inept offensive performance is Kaleb Johnson carried the ball five times for 35 yards in the second half. It wasn’t a case of one 20-yard run, one 12-yard run and three carries for 1 yard apiece. Instead, it was 6, 8, 9, 4 and 8.
“Yeah, I thought he did a nice job” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “I thought he was hitting the hole, running with good pad level, pressing the line of scrimmage, and you can kind of feel him a little bit. I thought that was a positive performance.”
He played one pass-protection snap and “showed the urgency” necessary to stuff Eric Wilson.
With Josh Jacobs coming back – perhaps against the Rams next week – the Packers might finally have a one-two punch with Jacobs and Johnson carrying the load and Chris Brooks getting the third-down snaps.
“I’m excited about that,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday. “Josh’s situation is kind of fluid – hopefully, we can get him back soon – but I think that would be good for our offense, for sure.”
The Packers don’t need to run the ball great. They just need to be able to run the ball so the play-action game has some teeth and provide advantageous down-and-distance situations.
The Packers aren’t going to find a combination on par with Washington’s famous Hogs or the bullying Eagles line that won the Super Bowl a couple years ago. All they need is a line physically able to not get destroyed in one-on-one situations and mentally capable of diagnosing blitzes.
Maybe the Packers will roll out that line against the Rams. Center Sean Rhyan might be back after missing most of the last four games with an ankle injury and Kevin Zeitler was set to get his crack at right guard before he was injured at practice last week. The mini-bye leading up to the Rams game could get him healthy.
An interior of Laken Tomlinson (or Aaron Banks), Rhyan and Zeitler might be good enough to open holes in the running game, protect Jordan Love and overcome the coaching.
“I think probably half the teams in the NFL are kind of dealing with what we’re dealing with, you know what I mean?” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “Just injuries, all the things that come with playing a season. You get to Week 10, Week 11, that’s just kind of what comes with it. Certain position groups, whether it’s the receivers, the o-line, the running backs, any position group in the NFL, you deal with this stuff.
“Is it ideal? Absolutely not. But that’s the situation, and we’ve got to embrace it and got to make the most of it. So that’s what we’re going to do.”
Micah Parsons had 12.5 sacks in the first 13 games of last season before he suffered a season-ending knee injury at Denver. Now, after a long comeback, he might make his debut against the Rams.
“Well, that’s my plan. I think my plan’s been different than everyone else’s this whole time,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “We’ll see. Obviously, having been in practice and banking some reps, there’s still a couple more hurdles for him to clear before we can definitely say that he’s a go. But he’s been showing progress and we’ll see where he’s at by the end of the week.”
Here are a few Micah Parsons clips from today pic.twitter.com/PdywEhndBD
Parsons is a Hall of Fame-level player. Along with all the sacks, he was fourth in pass-rush win rate. He was capable of making a game-changing play at any moment.
“I'm expecting him just to go out there and perform and help our football team win and execute at a high level,” edge coach and assistant head coach DeMarcus Covington said on Tuesday. “That's really what I'm managing those expectations on whatever. I do know he's Micah Parsons and he can do what he needs to do to help us win.”
There has to be reasonable expectations, though. Tucker Kraft hasn’t been the same dominant player since last year’s torn ACL. Parsons will be a game-changer – at times.
“I think it’s realistic and I think I’m going to have terrible plays,” Parsons said when he returned to practice. “I didn’t go through training camp. So, am I going to be the All-Pro Micah, the person I once was this year? Probably not until later, after I go through all my phases and things like that. …
“I think you’ll see flashes of All-Pro Micah when I get to pass rush, and there’s going to be times when you’re going to be like, ‘Dang, what was Micah doing?’ There’s going to be times when I question myself, too. Like, ‘What was I doing right there?’ I’m not ashamed of that. I’m not afraid of seeing the failure because I just came back from an 11-month injury. So, I’m not shying away from the possibility of my bad plays but I will look forward to is things that I do do good.”
The Packers enter their bye ranked second in the league with 20 takeaways – one behind Tampa Bay, three more than Minnesota and at least six more than 27 teams. Their streak of six consecutive games with at least two was snapped vs. the Vikings, when Xavier McKinney intercepted one pass and Karl Brooks had to settle for a sack after forcing an interception.
That’s a sustained run at taking away the ball, leading to belief that there’s some staying power that the Packers can force turnovers as the calendar turns to December and runs into January.
Moreover, of the final seven games, the Bears and Saints have the fifth-most giveaways, the Seahawks have the seventh-most, the Rams are tied for the ninth-most and the Bills are tied for the 11th-most.
There’s a reason why Jordan Love had moved into the top five of the MVP race after his bombs-away masterpiece against the Patriots. The production dropped off the cliff against the Vikings for a myriad of reasons, but he is a top-tier quarterback – and any team with a top-tier quarterback has a chance to win any game.
Love is a modest 12th with a 96.9 passer rating. Importantly, he’s a solid ninth in passer rating, seventh in completion percentage and fifth in yards per attempt when pressured. Not surprisingly given the number of pressures he’s faced, he’s first by a wide margin in yards when under duress.
If the Packers can keep Love on his feet, he along with his dynamic duo of receivers can carry the team into February.
No, the remaining schedule absolutely is not easy. Green Bay’s final seven opponents have a combined .547 winning percentage, which is tied for the sixth-toughest remaining slate of games. They will play four games against teams that have a winning record, along with a home game against the Texans, who have rallied a bit with three wins after a 0-4 start.
Instead, the highlight of the schedule for Green Bay is it won’t have to play the Vikings again until either the playoffs or next season. The Packers are 6-2 against teams not from Minnesota and might have been 7-1 if not for some dubious calls at Detroit.

title: Week 11 Consensus NFL Power Rankings: How Badly Were Packers Punished?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers might have been blown out of the NFC North championship race on Sunday, but they weren’t blown out of our Week 11 Consensus NFL Power Rankings.
Our Consensus Power Rankings take eight sets of national power rankings and turn them into one superior power ranking. The first-place team gets one point, the second-place team gets two points and so on.
After the Packers pummeled the Patriots for their fifth win in six games last week, they surged to 10th . After the Packers were pummeled by the Vikings on Sunday, they slid back only two spots to 12th.
The Bills are No. 1. The Packers’ NFC North rivals dominate the top 10, with Chicago fourth, Minnesota eighth and Detroit ninth. After the bye, the Packers will play at the Los Angeles Rams, who are 11th.
Here’s where you’ll find the Packers in each of the individual rankings, with more extensive analysis at the links.
Nick Shook is the only writer who has the Packers as a top-10 team . Barely, obviously, after he dropped them two spots and said the Packers are on the “edge of the quagmire” after their reliance on their big-play passing game was crushed by the Vikings.
“One might simply say the Vikings have the Packers' number; I tend to think Minnesota merely exposed a weakness that might hold back Green Bay as it fights to remain in the playoff hunt in the toughest division in football. That’s not enough to knock the Pack out of the top 10, but it does shake my confidence in them.”
The Packers inched back only two spots in Ralph Vacchiano’s rankings. The Packers were rolling until they were “completely bullied” by the Vikings’ defense.
“Sure, it’s just one game against a really good team, but the Packers are now two games back in the loss column of the three other NFC North teams. Green Bay has the bye week to think about that before trying to get back on its feet in two weeks in Los Angeles against the Rams.”
The Packers plummeted seven spots from No. 5 in Conor Orr’s rankings.
“At the end of the day, after several beautiful and frantic Jordan Love games, the truth is this: The Packers’ offensive line cannot handle a defensive front like Minnesota’s. Period. Love had one of the fastest snap to throw times in the NFL this past weekend. It. Did. Not. Matter.”
The Packers were pummeled but only fell one spot in ESPN’s rankings , which are selected by its team beat writers.
This week’s theme is non-quarterback midseason MVP, with Rob Demovsky picking receiver Christian Watson, who referenced his contract extension that seemed questionable because of his limited production and injury issues.
“Now that Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in touchdown catches (seven), a deal that doesn't even rank him among the top 20 highest-paid receivers in terms of average per year looks pretty good.”
The Packers fell three spots in the rankings selected by Chad Graff and Josh Kendall. Their breakout player is Christian Watson.
“The ambulance clip alone gives Watson the nod here, but the fifth-year wide receiver is having a career year on top of that. Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in receiving touchdowns (seven). Watson had not topped 620 receiving yards in any of his previous four seasons.”
The Packers tumbled four spots in Frank Schwab’s rankings. There are “concerns” after getting smashed by the Vikings, namely on the offensive line and a limited running game. However, the “bye comes at a good time,” he said.
“They were playing very well before Sunday, when they were crushed at home by the Vikings. The break gives the Packers a chance to regroup, and also perhaps get Micah Parsons back for a game against the Rams the day before Thanksgiving. The Packers should rightly believe that Parsons will transform their team upon his return.”
The Packers tumbled three spots in Pete Prisco’s rankings.
“The offensive line was a disaster against the Vikings,” he wrote. “That led to quarterback Jordan Love being abused all day, which can't happen if they are to be a playoff team.”
The Packers dipped two spots in Mike Florio’s rankings. He said the Packers “desperately” need a running game.
The Packers will (sort of) have their bye this week. It won’t be a full week off, though, with the Packers playing at the Rams on Wednesday. That means they’ll be on the practice field on Saturday, Sunday and Monday, on a plane on Tuesday and on the field on Wednesday.
The Rams are at No. 11 in the Consensus Power Rankings. They are No. 12 in Ralph Vacchiano’s rankings at Fox Sports, one spot behind the Packers. As part of a longer summary, he wrote:
“Don’t look now, but the supposed Dream Team has won four straight to salvage some respectability out of their season and maybe, just maybe, turn them into a threat again. The way the Rams are hemorrhaging players, it might be too little, too late. They will be without their two best wideouts, Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, for a while, and they’ve got the Packers, Chiefs, 49ers, Cowboys and Seahawks lined up when they come out of their bye week.”
Sportsbook odds are not used in our rankings, but they do provide an additional insight on how the teams are viewed. In Packers-related odds at FanDuel Sportsbook :
The Packers were +2000 to win the Super Bowl at the start of the season, crashed to +6000 after their slow start and finally rebounded to status quo after beating New England. However, they’re back to +3000 after losing to Minnesota. That’s 12th on the board and behind all the NFC North teams, with Chicago at +800, Minnesota at +1400 and Detroit at +2000.
Green Bay opened the season ranked seventh in the NFC playoff odds, fell to as low as +250 but were -230 after beating New England. Now, they are +128, which ranks eighth in the NFC.
Quarterback Jordan Love’s express train to NFL MVP was derailed. At FanDuel , Love opened at +2200, crashed to as long as +10000 but was fifth on the board at +700 after dropping a series of bombs on the Patriots. Now, he’s +5000, which ranks seventh.
The Packers are viewed as completely out of the NFC North race . The Vikings with Kirk Cousins are +145, the Bears are +175 and the Lions without Aidan Hutchinson are +250. The Packers are the caboose at a distant +2700.

title: Latest NFC Standings, Projections Show Packers Might Have Dug Playoff Grave
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Had the Green Bay Packers beaten the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, they would have taken a big step out of the seventh-seed pit they’ve been stuck in the last three years.
Now, it might be seventh seed or bust.
Here’s a look at the NFC playoff standings at the end of Week 10.
1. San Francisco 49ers, 8-1.
3. New York Giants, 5-3-1.
4. Carolina Panthers, 4-5.
The Three Wild-Card Front-Runners
5. Minnesota Vikings, 7-2.
7. Green Bay Packers, 6-4.
In the Hunt Because of Lousy Divisions
11. Washington Commanders, 3-5-1.
12. Tampa Bay Buccaneers, 3-6.
13. New Orleans Saints, 3-6.
15. Arizona Cardinals, 3-7.
16. Philadelphia Eagles, 2-7.
Had the Packers beaten the Vikings, they would have been in the No. 6 spot in the NFC and just a half-game behind the Lions, who they’ll host in Week 18, and the Bears, who they beat earlier this season. That would have placed the NFC North championship and a move up to the No. 2 seed – meaning a home game in the wild-card round with the potential of another in the divisional round – within their grasp.
Instead, the Packers are clinging to the No. 7 spot because of a flimsy tiebreaker. Seattle is No. 8 and Los Angeles is No. 9 because Seattle has the better NFC West record. Thus, the Seahawks rank ahead of the Rams, but the Packers are ahead of the Seahawks because of a better record in conference games.
With eight weeks left in the season, the tiebreakers are subject to change.
In this case, the tiebreakers are irrelevant.
After this week’s phony-baloney bye, the Packers will visit the Rams on Thanksgiving Eve. The winner, obviously, will be 7-4 and own the head-to-head tiebreaker. The loser, obviously, will be 6-5, so one game behind officially but really two games behind because of the tiebreaker.
So, it won’t be a must-win game for the Packers but it’s not too far off.
“Oh, for sure,” quarterback Jordan Love said after the game about being behind the 8-ball in the playoff race. “We’ve talked about [how] these are the games you’ve got to win – NFC North games, and we’re 1-3 in the North. So, yeah, we’ve got to obviously just keep rolling, take it one week at a time, like we’ve talked about.
“But we’ve dropped the ball in three of these games, obviously – two against the Vikings, one against the Lions – that you’ve got to win these games to have a chance in this division. Obviously, we talk about, ‘Everybody’s good, everybody’s winning.’ So, it starts with the division games. You’ve got to handle business, and we didn’t do that today.”
The No. 7 seed is a bad spot to be in because it means a wild-card game at the No. 2 seed and a potential divisional-round game at the No. 1 seed. But, at this point, the No. 7 speed would be better than nothing.
According to Tankathon , the Bears have the toughest remaining strength of schedule, with their eight opponents having a combined .630 winning percentage. The Rams are next at .597, with the Packers fifth at .547, the Seahawks seventh at .538, the Lions eighth at .534 and the Vikings 10th at .527.
So, once again, the Packers blew a huge opportunity against the Vikings. They would have been hot on the heels of the NFC North front-runners, all of whom have difficult closing schedules.
Remaining Strength of Schedule pic.twitter.com/gpSDHvHqyH
In the seventh-or-bust race, the Packers’ remaining schedule includes games against the Rams, Bills, Lions and Bears. The Rams have two games left against the Seahawks along with the Packers, 49ers and Chiefs. The Seahawks have the two games against the Rams along with the 49ers and Giants.
The Packers and Rams will have the equivalent of a mini-bye to get ready for their Thanksgiving Eve showdown.
“Certainly, we’re all disappointed by the product we put out there yesterday,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “When you’re playing a good football team, you can’t lose the turnover battle like that. We knew that was a critical element going into the game. They were 6-0 when they won the ball; now, they’re 7-0.
“It’ll give our guys a chance to reset, gives us a chance as a coaching staff to try to put together the best plan possible, because we know we got a really good football team in the Rams. I know they’re beat up in some spots, but I think there’s no disputing they’re one of the best teams in the National Football League.”
Here’s what the computers say about the Packers’ playoff chances.
According to The Athletic’s Playoff Predictor before last week’s games, the Packers had a 64 percent chance of qualifying for the playoffs, with a 13 percent chance of winning the division. At the time, a win would have moved the Packers’ playoff chances to 76 percent and loss would have sent them down to 46 percent.
Instead, the Packers have a 35 percent chance.
If the Packers can beat the Rams, that would rebound to 58 percent. With a loss, it would fall even further to 23 percent.
At ESPN , the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs. With a win, that would have improved to 75 percent; with a loss, that would have fallen to 45 percent. Instead, it plunged to 33 percent.
At NFL.com , the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs. Instead of 74 percent with a win and 45 percent with a loss, their playoff probability is down to 34 percent.
At Playoff Status , the Packers had a 66 percent chance of reaching the playoffs. Instead of 87 percent with a win and 56 percent with a loss, their playoff chances fell to 47 percent.
Using Stick to the Model ’s Playoff Machine, the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs, with a swing of 72 percent with a win over Minnesota but 40 percent with a loss. Instead, their playoff probability tumbled to 35 percent.
“I think you’ve got to take it one week at a time,” Love said. “We’re 6-4, so it’s not like we have a losing record. We got to obviously just overcome, take it one week at a time, and win games. But it’s a disappointing loss, and like I said, you just got to get back to work.”
The LaFleur-Love teams have been good during their three-plus years together. They’ve never been great. The Packers' loss to the Vikings was the latest example, writes @JacobWestendorf . ⬇️ https://t.co/uBFicTGOLQ

title: Texans Have No Excuse Not to Sign Justin Reid After Saints Release
full_text:
In a bit of surprising news that surfaced ahead of the NFL's Week 11 action, the New Orleans Saints are expected to release two-time Super Bowl champion safety Justin Reid, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
Sources: The #Saints are planning to grant the release requested by safety Justin Reid, as both sides agreed this would be mutually beneficial. Reid, a 2x Super Bowl champion, is just 29 years old and has 698 total tackles, 11 INTs, 52 pass deflections, 6.5 sacks, 3 forced… pic.twitter.com/vahHoVZRZ6
Reid, who has been with the Saints for the past two seasons as a solid starting safety and team captain, seemingly didn't have a long-term role in New Orleans moving forward.
His snap share had dipped over the last three weeks. The Saints as a whole were struggling, and as a result, the two sides have parted ways despite Reid having one year left on his existing contract.
So now, the door becomes wide open for Reid to look around the market for a new team to call home for the second half of the 2026 season. Schultz reports that Reid is looking to sign with a contender, thus shrinking the pool of candidates to sign him to those with a realistic route for a playoff appearance.
Immediately, one team that sticks out as a strong suitor–– even with a 4-6 record–– is Reid's former team, the Houston Texans; a team that's building momentum at the right time for a late-season run to the playoffs , but could also use the extra help at safety with an experienced veteran like Reid.
Throughout the first half of the Texans' season, their defense has lacked the true elite production that they had proven to be capable of over the course of last year. Their consistency within the back-end of their secondary has been a big component of those struggles.
While Calen Bullock has held his own, it's been that second safety spot that's been an issue for the Texans across most of the season.
Reed Blankenship has seemingly regressed from his time with the Philadelphia Eagles and has struggled to adjust in his new situation, while his backup, M.J. Stewart, hasn't been much of an upgrade himself when he's been elevated as a starter.
Those back-end woes became so much of a concern for the Texans that rumors surfaced at the trade deasdline linking the team to interest in acquiring a safety.
That move ultimately didn't happen, yet it did show that Houston might've been interested in adding another contributor to the position to  help raise their floor from where things have stood through the first half of the regular season.
However, only a few weeks after the deadline has passed, and a starting-level safety in Justin Reid has now emerged on the market that the Texans could sign as a low-risk, high-reward addition to their secondary.
Now, throughout the first half of the season, Reid has not played particularly well compared to some of his prior years.
Pro Football Focus puts him at an overall grade of 49.1 that nearly ranks in the bottom 10 of eligible safeties. He's allowed 24 receptions with 12.5 yards per catch, has 11 missed tackles, and a not-so-great 141.7 passer rating when targeted.
At the same time, he is an experienced, veteran safety who the Texans could simply roll into the mix as a rotational piece in their secondary. He's a physical presence who can support the run rather well, and he was a former team captain from his time in New Orleans; all of which are traits that Houston values in any defensive back.
For a team that has struggled at the safety position like the Texans have this year, adding Reid is a risk worth taking.
Houston has over $8 million in available salary cap spending and could add on the nine-year veteran to a rest-of-season deal in an attempt that he can, at the very least, add depth and run support to a position that has been underwhelming for most of the season.
Worst case scenario: the Texans add Reid, realize he's not a great fit or the player he once was, turn back to either Blankenship or Stewart , and revert back to the status quo.
Best case scenario: he adds security to the back-end of Houston's secondary, becomes a weekly starter next to Bullock, and helps patch a hole that has consistently plagued this defense over the course of the season.
Regardless, a signing of the former Texans safety is a clear aggressive push from this front office that shows they still have belief in what this team could do in the second half of the season.
For a team that had real Super Bowl expectations heading into Week 1, at the very least, it's a move to seriously consider to try and keep building momentum to close out the year on a high note.

title: Texans' TNF Snap Counts Show Big Changes for Nico Collins, 2 Rookies
full_text:
The Houston Texans claimed a much-needed victory over the Indianapolis Colts on Thursday Night Football that might end up as the necessary spark to help this Texans team rattle off a few wins in a row over the coming weeks.
And in the aftermath of the Texans' win over their division rival Colts, we're now able to take a glance at the snap counts for both sides in the midst of Thursday night's action, and pick apart a few aspects that stand out from Houston's side of the equation.
Let's take a look at how those snap counts unraveled, then break down five key notes from how the Texans' lineup decisions panned out.
It may not seem like much, but Nico Collins seeing around 90% of the Texans' offensive snaps is something we haven't seen much of this season. The number actually sets his season-high in snaps through his eight appearances on the year.
Normally, Collins is on the field for a little under 75% of the Texans' total offensive looks. But over the past two weeks, Houston's star wideout has seen over 85%. Before Week 10, his highest on the season was 73% against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Perhaps it's because of the multiple injuries to the wide receiver position, or simply because the coaching staff wants to feature Collins more than he has been this season. Whatever the reason is, it's resulted in back-to-back weeks of over 50 yards and a touchdown.
The Texans have been forced to make a change in their linebacker unit over the past two weeks due to Azeez Al-Shaair's injured reserve placement. And at first, it seemed as if Jake Hansen was in line to claim most of his snaps to start next to Henry To'oTo'o.
And Hansen did see over 60% of the defensive snaps in this game. However, fourth-round rookie linebacker Wade Woodaz also stepped up for a 32% snap share on the defensive side, his highest on the season so far.
Maybe that increased involvement from Woodaz is a sign of things to come after the Texans come off their mini-bye. Woodaz finished those 16 snaps with two solo tackles.
Another rookie who stepped up and saw some of his highest share of opportunities for the season: second round tight end Marlin Klein, who finally became a more featured component of the Texans' offense with a 24% snap share.
And the Texans made sure to give Klein his fair share of targets when he was on the field. Klein converted on all four of his targets for four catches, 24 yards, and his first-career touchdown thanks to a 13-yard red-zone reception sent in by C.J. Stroud.
Klein still found himself as third in the pecking order at tight end behind Dalton Schultz and Foster Moreau. But considering Klein was a weekly healthy scratch only a few weeks ago, this is certainly a step in the right direction for his development.
DeMeco Ryans explained after the win that the Texans had planned to rotate their right tackle spot between Braden Smith and Trent Brown before Brown would go down with a back injury early in the game.
That back injury left Brown to just seven snaps. As for Smith, though, he saw a season-high 59 offensive snaps and played pretty well in the process. He came out to an 88.1 overall grade via Pro Football Focus, excelling as a run blocker while also allowing just two pressures and zero sacks in pass protection.
Considering how well David Montgomery was running the ball, paired with his production as a pass-blocker, it might be hard to pull Smith out of the mix as a starter now. We'll see how the Texans approach things upfront once Week 12 arrives.
After M.J. Stewart had stepped up as the Texans' starting safety next to Calen Bullock over the last three weeks, the Texans made a pivot in their secondary against the Colts ; Reed Blankenship would fill back into his starting spot after seemingly being benched in Week 10 after recovering from his hand injury.
As for Stewart, he saw zero defensive snaps, instead filling into a more frequent part of the special teams unit with over 80% of Houston's total special teams snaps.
