title: Saints Find Another Way to Lose as Panthers Steal NFC South Victory
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints had chance after chance to build momentum and secure their first consecutive wins of the season. Instead, it was another game that left a sour taste in everyone’s mouths like tomatoes in gumbo.
Kicker Ryan Fitzgerald connected on a game-winning 54-yard field goal as time expired, lifting the Carolina Panthers to a 20-17 victory over the Saints on Sunday afternoon at the Caesars Superdome.
The loss dropped New Orleans to 3-6 under second-year head coach Kellen Moore , while Carolina improved to 4-5 and strengthened its position in the NFC South standings.
Despite overcoming a sluggish first half and taking a fourth-quarter lead, the Saints couldn't finish the job, and Carolina escaped with a crucial divisional win.
Tyler Shough went 25-for-36 for 187 yards, with a touchdown and an interception, while rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson had a breakout game, leading New Orleans with 11 receptions for 80 yards.
Running back Alvin Kamara provided the Saints' biggest offensive spark, scoring twice in the second half on a 3-yard touchdown run in the third quarter and a 4-yard touchdown catch in the fourth.
However, New Orleans struggled offensively throughout the opening two quarters, committing two turnovers and failing to score before halftime.
Shough's first interception came on the Saints' opening possession when cornerback Marco Wilson deflected his fourth-down pass intended for Chris Olave , and linebacker Devin Lloyd intercepted it.
The Saints' defense kept Carolina from capitalizing, with Carl Granderson sacking Bryce Young on fourth down near the goal line.
Another costly mistake came in the second quarter when Shough and Audric Estime mishandled a handoff, allowing Panthers linebacker Jaelan Phillips to recover the fumble.
Carolina capitalized on the turnover with a 2-yard touchdown run by Chuba Hubbard , taking a 7-0 lead into halftime.
New Orleans finally found some traction in the third quarter.
Kamara capped a nine-play, 64-yard drive with a 3-yard touchdown run, tying the game at 7-7 with 6:33 remaining in the period.
However, Fitzgerald answered with a 55-yard field goal to restore Carolina's three-point advantage entering the fourth quarter.
The Saints responded with their best offensive sequence of the afternoon.
Shough connected with Kamara on a 4-yard touchdown pass, giving New Orleans its first lead at 14-10.
That advantage proved short-lived.
Hubbard scored his second touchdown on a 1-yard run, putting Carolina back ahead 17-14 late in the fourth quarter.
New Orleans refused to go away, with kicker Charlie Smyth drilling a clutch 55-yard field goal to tie the game at 17-17.
But Young and the Panthers orchestrated one final scoring opportunity, setting up Fitzgerald's game-winning kick as time expired.
Young finished with 200 passing yards, while Hubbard rushed for 92 yards and two touchdowns on 27 carries.
For the Saints, the defeat represents another frustrating setback in a season defined by inconsistency, offensive mistakes and an inability to capitalize on opportunities.
The Saints will now prepare for a road trip to the Buckeye State to take on the Cincinnati Bengals .

I think this will be a relatively close game for the Saints.
While the defense is flawed in some areas, New Orleans arguably has the best pass rush duo in Chase Young and Carl Granderson , who are both in the top five in sacks. However, I’m still worried about its inability to stop the run, especially when the opposing team has a solid running back. Unfortunately for the Saints, Carolina has a pretty dadgum good running back in Chuba Hubbard , who has rushed for 619 yards and reached paydirt five times this season.
On top of that, the Saints’ defense will go up against a better quarterback in Bryce Young , who has thrown for 2,197 yards with 18 touchdowns and six interceptions and is the face of the fourth-best passing attack in the NFL and one that features wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan (46 receptions, 625 yards, 3 touchdowns).
The good thing for the Saints is that the Panthers aren’t the greatest defense when it comes to stopping the run as they are 28th in the league in rushing yards allowed. The Saints were able to run the ball effectively last week against the Cleveland Browns , who also had a similar issue, but execution will be key.
Can the Saints pull off the win and remain in first place? It’s definitely a possibility.
However, I cannot trust Kellen Moore’s ability to manage and put together a game plan for four quarters because Tyler Shough and the Saints have won three games despite the offensive staff’s ineptitude.
Also, add on the fact that the Saints are missing two of their starting offensive linemen on an already porous offensive line in center Erik McCoy and right tackle Taliese Fuaga , the Saints’ chances of winning decrease.

On Sunday, the Saints and Panthers play for first place in the NFC South in the Superdome. Admittedly, both teams have three wins in their eight games, but first place is on the line, nonetheless. It's hard to believe, but it was just 2021 that Tampa Bay , a team tied for the bottom of this division, won it all.
Point being, things change rapidly in this professional sport Americans love so much.

title: Giants Offense Faces a Tough Test Against Jaguars' Ball-Hawking Defense
full_text:
The New York Giants offense will face another tough test this Sunday against the Jacksonville Jaguars defense.
The unit is led by defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile, who has built one of the best run defenses in the NFL. Add an opportunistic, aggressive secondary, and you have a dangerous group.
It's a challenge the Giants' offensive brain trust must be prepared to handle, or it will be a long day for Big Blue Nation fans. Jacksonville allows 16 points per game, the second-best mark in the NFL. Let's explore this defense further.
The Jaguars do their damage from an even front. While they will come out in a 4-3 look, they primarily play a 4-2-5 to combat the more pass-happy offenses seen around the league today.
In those situations, they normally have two legitimate edge rushers on the field, along with two run-stuffing interior defensive linemen and two off-ball linebackers.
That front is flanked by five defensive backs, allowing the Jaguars to maneuver and change their looks depending on the offense's formations.
The Jaguars have the sixth-ranked rushing defense in the NFL. They allow 91 yards per game and a paltry 3.3 yards per carry, and they have surrendered only five rushing touchdowns all season.
Foye Oluokun is the driving force in the center of the defense. He and fellow linebacker Ventrell Miller have combined for 122 tackles, including 74 solo stops and nine tackles for loss.
Former Philadelphia Eagle Jordan Davis will make his debut for this defense after spending a week acclimating to the system. This season, he has 31 total tackles in nine games, following 72 total tackles in 2025.
That type of production on the interior is bound to make things more difficult for opposing offensive linemen. His addition next to defensive tackle Davon Godchaux will make it extremely difficult for New York to run between the tackles.
Davis's presence will be felt not only against the run but also in the passing game. The Jaguars currently rank 19th in passing defense, surrendering 229 yards per game, but they have also intercepted 12 passes.
In addition to Davis as an interior pass rusher, the Jaguars acquired All-Pro safety Jessie Bates from the Atlanta Falcons, who also spent Week 10 acclimating himself to the defensive system. Both should help bolster what is already a plucky and mischievous pass defense.
Travis Hunter leads the secondary and is what happens when you put elite WR1 skills on the defensive side of the ball. He has three interceptions already and is one of three defensive backs who make it extremely difficult for offenses to throw.
Jourdan Lewis is tied with Hunter for the team lead with three interceptions, while Jarrian Jones leads the team with eight passes defensed. Adding an All-Pro in his prime to this defensive backfield should help it reach the next level.
The Jaguars have a lot of names on the injury report. Defensive linemen Danny Striggow, Matt Dickerson and Arik Armstead pepper the injury wire, but when Travon Walker pops up, it raises eyebrows.
He has been dealing with a rib injury and has been limited in practice this week. If he doesn't play, it is a major hit to their ability to set the edge in the run game and provide pressure without bringing extra defenders.
Three words describe what the Giants' offense needs to do to succeed against the Jaguars: "Control the middle!"
The Giants' interior offensive line has to do a good job handling Davis and Godchaux inside. It also needs to work up to the second level and get bodies on the interior linebackers.
The Giants must continue to target Isaiah Likely in the middle of the field. That will keep the linebackers from selling out against the run, since they'll be afraid Likely may get behind them over the top.
Ultimately, they need to keep the safeties high at the third level by attacking the middle of the field deep with post routes and pipe routes. That opens up the seams and the outside corner or flag areas.

title: Giants 2027 NFL Draft Watchlist: Four College Prospects to Observe This Weekend
full_text:
As the New York Giants (5-3-1) prepare to host the Jacksonville Jaguars (7-2) for a Week 11 showdown at MetLife Stadium, several Big Blue scouts will be watching closely on college football’s Week 12 slate.
While several potential targets make their case for being selected in the 2027 NFL Draft, the team’s biggest needs are becoming clearer.
In addition to their most pressing need at defensive tackle, coach John Harbaugh and his staff may also want to add players who can bolster their depth charts at running back and at tight end.
Here are four players the Giants may be keeping an eye on this weekend.
Despite leaving Miami’s 36-25 win over Duke last week with a right lower-body injury, Fletcher is off the Hurricanes’ injury report and is expected to play this weekend against Virginia Tech.
With just two regular-season contests remaining, the Fort Lauderdale native should be eager to showcase his talents to potential suitors.
Fletcher has compiled 537 rushing yards and 10 rushing touchdowns, while averaging 4.7 yards per carry this season. His 36 career rushing scores give him the Miami Hurricanes program record.
At 6-foot-2, 225 pounds, Fletcher is the type of physical, downhill runner who can thrive as the lead back in offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s system. Drawing comparisons to Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry, Fletcher could provide the Giants with the primary ball carrier they've been seeking to pair with current starter Cam Skattebo.
Few, if any, draft prospects define the term ‘raw potential’ better than Brownlow-Dindy. The Lakeland, FL native’s value to the Gamecocks extends far beyond his nine total tackles this season. As a result, he will be looking to showcase his talents against the top-ranked Georgia Bulldogs this weekend.
Despite spending much of his collegiate career as a rotational defensive tackle, the 6-foot-3, 310-pound lineman has the frame to absorb opposing double teams and the initial burst to shed blocks. He also has surprising lateral agility for a player his size, making him a versatile piece along the interior defensive line.
Brownlow-Dindy, who projects best as either a 1-tech nose tackle or a 3-tech lineman at the pro level, could provide the Giants with some much-needed depth along the defensive front. Once considered a five-star recruit, he has the skills to earn a starting role, but it will take time to cultivate his untapped potential.
Given New York’s difficulty in consistently stopping the run, Gracial could be an enticing mid-to-late-round option for the Giants. In five appearances for the Tigers this season, he has logged nine total tackles and 3.5 tackles for loss. He will look to increase those totals this weekend against Kentucky.
At 6-foot-4, 320 pounds, Gracial is at his best when using his strength and solid build to overpower opposing run-blockers. He plays with good leverage and has the early-snap quickness to invade opposing backfields.
Should New York bring him into the fold, Gracial has the skill set to improve their run defense immediately. Though he still needs to improve at generating pressure on the passer, the St. Louis native would satisfy Big Blue’s need for depth along the interior of the defensive line.
While Giants’ scouts are keeping a close eye on Miami’s Mark Fletcher, Jr. on Saturday, they may also want to pay attention to the Hokies’ top tight end.
Reynolds enters this matchup having compiled 585 receiving yards and six touchdowns. The 6-foot-4, 250-pound tight end has the ideal blend of speed and short-area agility needed to succeed in an NFL passing offense. Reynolds can also add notable yards after the catch while giving Virginia Tech a reliable target on fourth-down conversions.
With New York’s depth at the position uncertain beyond starter Isaiah Likely, Reynolds could be a highly productive fit within offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense. A strong showing against the Hurricanes in Week 12 would go a long way toward bolstering his draft stock.

title: Giants Mailbag: Possible Cap Casualties, Return-Man Worries and O-Line Questions
full_text:
Welcome to the weekly New York Giants On SI mailbag! From offseason moves to game-day strategies, we'll do our best to answer your questions. (Some questions have been edited for brevity and clarity.)
From Wayne C. (via email): I know you do a lot of cap work, so I was wondering if you had any early thoughts on which contracts the Giants might purge in the offseason and what the savings would be. Thanks.
Wayne, the first contract I think goes is cornerback Paulson Adebo’s. He has a $20.317 million cap figure next year, and if they trim that contract, they’d save $14 million (which I’ve often said could go toward the franchise tag for Deonte Banks if they want to keep him)
I also wonder if they give up on Chauncey Golston, who has dealt with injuries two years in a row. Doing so would save $5.5 million in cap space if they move on from him. And I have to think the defensive line is going to be a top priority in the draft.
I don’t particularly like to get too excited one way or another about next year’s cap space , but the Giants, per Over the Cap, have$ 18.969 million in total space, $1.927 million in projected effective cap space (what they have left to fit guys under the Top 51 once that rule begins on the first day of the new league year)
I think the Giants will do some restructures—I’d like to see them try to lower Brian Burns’ number ( $44.083 million in 2027 ) via an extension. I also think they should do something with Andrew Thomas’s number ( $29.952 million ).
What do they see in Theo Johnson.  He used to be annoying with the drops, now the coaches are annoying for throwing to them at all and expecting better results
Jonny,  if I were to guess, they see a guy with a blend of size, straight-line speed, and red-zone physicality that can be weaponized in the seam.
Johnson is also versatile enough to be moved around the formation. However, what he hasn't been is consistent, both in route running and in blocking.
And quite frankly, I'm intrigued by what Thomas Fidone II has shown. He flashes, as I recall, during the summer. I wouldn't mind seeing more of what he can do.
From Kevin C. via e-mail: I'm wondering how much confidence you have in Xavier Gipson making returns, given his woeful history of losing the ball. Personally, I'll be holding my breath every time I see him settling under a kick. I'm not sorry to see Charlie Jones relieved of the duty, but it's hard to believe that Gipson is the best they can do.
Kevin, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t have concerns. This almost reminds me of the kicker odyssey from recent years. And not for nothing, but with the weather supposed to be soggy on Sunday, I’m definitely concerned about ball security. Hopefully it will be uneventful.
From Isaac S. via e-mail: The Giants offensive line hasn’t been as consistent as last year. What do you attribute that to, and how would you fix it?
Isaac, per PFF, the Giants are tied for the fifth-best pass-blocking efficiency rating in the league with the 49ers, each team holding an 88.0 PBE .
The Giants, remember, have had both of their tackles (Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor) banged up for most of the season, so I’m sure that has been a factor in terms of breakdowns.
I also think Francis Mauigoa’s transition from guard to tackle has been bumpy. He’s still learning the position, and I think in time he’s going to be very good. But there are clear growing pains he has to work through right now.
I think the way to fix any concerns is first to keep developing the depth behind the starters, J.C. Davis and Marcus Mbow. I also think they add another center next year, possibly in free agency, since I don't see them re-signing John Michael Schmitz.
From Peter D. (via e-mail): The Jags are good, with two new defensive stars coming. Their wins include the Browns, Pats, Eagles, Colts, and Titans, and they lost to the Texans. They've beaten good teams, but I am not awed by what I see. Eliminate turnovers and penalties, minimize mistakes, and a win is not impossible. Your thoughts?
I think you summed it up nicely , Peter. There's really not much I can add.

title: Former Giants Tre Hawkins III and Turbo Miller Land With UFL Champs and Runner-Up
full_text:
Unfortunately, neither running back Dante “Turbo” Miller nor cornerback Tre Hawkins III had much success during their tenures with the New York Giants .
They didn’t end up in the organization’s long-term plans, but their football dreams may not be done yet .
Both men heard their names called in the 2027 United Football League Draft, and they landed on the two teams that competed in last season’s title game.
The reigning champion Louisville Kings selected Hawkins in the fourth round (No. 32 overall), and the runner-up DC Defenders took Miller in the 12th (No. 95).
The UFL, which has eight teams and begins play in late March, can offer NFL castoffs a welcome chance to continue their professional careers. Those who stand out could find themselves on a training camp roster next summer.
Hawkins and Miller are no strangers to adversity, so fans shouldn’t write them off yet.
New York took a chance on Hawkins in the sixth round of the 2023 NFL Draft and gave him a decent look during his rookie season. The 6-foot-3 corner registered 35 combined tackles in 17 games and was an asset in the limited coverage snaps he was given.
Hawkins had a path to a solid role in the secondary, but he fractured his lumbar spine in December 2024. He was waived before the 2025 season and tried to make a comeback with the Washington Commanders.
The Temple, Texas, native has played only one game since last November and spent less than a week with the Minnesota Vikings before being cut at the end of August. This is a violent sport that can shorten careers and lives.
Hawkins is getting another chance to continue his passion. Hopefully, he will stay healthy with the Kings.
Miller, who went undrafted in 2024, generated hype for his exceptional speed and cool name, but he couldn’t squeeze his way into the backfield on game days. The 5-foot-9, 200-pound running back had no touches during his on-and-off two-year stint with the organization.
If Miller can flash his natural ability in D.C., an NFL team may decide to scoop him up. Given most executives’ aversion to paying top dollar for the position, running back depth is valuable.
Misfortune factored into Hawkins’ and Miller’s departures. They were easy to root for, which makes their circumstances even more disappointing.
They remain connected to the gridiron, however, and will be looking for a way back to the NFL.
There is no reason to obsess over the future, though. They can showcase their skills and endless tenacity in the UFL, and that is something to be thankful for this holiday season.

title: Daniel Jones Won’t Get a Revenge Game Against the Giants After Colts Release Him
full_text:
There will be no revenge game for quarterback Daniel Jones when the New York Giants visit the Indianapolis Colts a week from Sunday.
Jones, the Colts’ former starting quarterback, was one year into a new two-year, $88 million contract when the team released him after another dismal showing, a 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans.
Before his release, Jones, the sixth overall pick by the Giants in the 2019 draft, had been on a historic run of futility.
Per Doug Clawson , Jones is the only quarterback in the past 45 years to start each of his team’s first 11 games of a season without a single game in which he threw more touchdown passes than interceptions.
In six seasons with the Giants, Jones appeared in 70 games, started 69 and went 24-44-1. He completed 64.1% of his passes for 14,582 yards and threw 70 touchdowns to 47 interceptions.
He missed most of the 2023 season with a torn ACL. In 2024, after the Giants’ overtime loss to the Carolina Panthers in Germany in Week 10, he was demoted as the starter, triggering an injury-protection clause in his contract, and was later released.
After a stint with the Vikings, he signed with the Colts as a free agent the following year and led them to an 8-5 record in 2025. As with the Giants, though, Jones had only one good season in Indianapolis.
The Colts are in the midst of a horrific season at 3-8. Per NFL insider Jordan Schultz, they received trade inquiries for Jones at the trade deadline but held on to him because they believed they had paid too much in bonus money.
Even so, the Colts took apart parts of their core, trading offensive lineman Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks, defensive lineman DeForest Buckner to the 49ers, receiver Keenan Allen to the 49ers and receiver Josh Downs to the Chiefs.
The Giants host the Jacksonville Jaguars at MetLife Stadium this week, then travel to face the Colts the following week.
"I don't want to get ahead of ourselves here, and you just hit me with that," Giants head coach John Harbaugh said when asked about the move made by the Colts, who will start Anthony Richardson, Sr. at quarterback when the Giants come to town.
"Definitely, the offense will be the offense that they run, but it'll be centered around the quarterback for sure, and they're probably different styles to some degree, so we'll have to look at that when the time comes. We have people doing that this week."

title: How the Giants Can Slow Down Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars
full_text:
Going into Week 11, the New York Giants face the 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars, an extremely tough opponent. Under head coach Liam Coen and offensive coordinator Grant Udinski, Jacksonville has developed the NFL’s fourth-highest-scoring offense, averaging 29.9 points per game.
Jacksonville’s base offense is 11 personnel. The Jaguars have an abundance of receiving weapons that let them make their 11 personnel look different from other offenses’.
They also have multiple backs with varying running styles who can operate in a one-back offense. You will see them go to 12 personnel on occasion to throw in a wrinkle and disrupt a defensive game plan.
This offense wants to establish the run. The Jaguars rank fourth in the NFL in rushing attempts, whether to establish their identity at the start of the game or to run out the clock at the end.
The rushing attack is a big part of their game. They have run the ball 266 times so far this season. Their 117.8 yards per game is good for 12th in the NFL, and they rank 11th in EPA per run play.
They are led by Bhayshul Tuten, the former Virginia Tech Hokie, who has taken over the backfield lead after Travis Etienne’s departure.
This offseason, he was joined by Chris Rodriguez Jr., who came over from Washington after learning Liam Coen’s offense at Kentucky. Their 4.0 yards per carry is decent, but it ranks 22nd among NFL teams, so the ground game is not an extremely potent weapon.
After exploding for the best stretch of his career toward the end of the 2025 season, Trevor Lawrence has hit the ground running this year as the undisputed leader of this passing attack.
He has been diplomatic with the ball, finding weapons all over the field and making it difficult for defenses to key in and shut down the passing attack because he isn’t locked in on one receiver.
Parker Washington has been the best of the bunch and the team’s most explosive element, but only because Travis Hunter isn’t a full-time member of the offense.
Brian Thomas Jr., the former LSU receiver who broke out during his rookie campaign, has seen his momentum fade and is now just another member of the group. Receiver Jakobi Meyers and tight end Brenton Strange provide options that defenses have to deal with.
Their 241.1 passing yards per game rank 11th in the NFL, but their 21 touchdown passes put them among the league’s best. They are second in both net yards per attempt and EPA per pass play.
With opening-day starting left tackle Anton Harrison on injured reserve, Walker Little has stepped in and anchored this offensive line.
He has protected Lawrence’s blind side in the passing game and has been a solid contributor as a run blocker.
The interior offensive line has also stepped up, with right guard Ezra Cleveland the most consistent in both the run game and pass protection.
Meanwhile, rookie Emmanuel Pregnon has continued to improve at left guard.
All three of the Jaguars’ running backs, Tuten, Rodriguez Jr. and LeQuint Allen, have been dealing with injuries.
Tuten’s injury looks serious enough that he could miss time on Sunday. If all three running backs are banged up, that works in favor of the Giants, who have shown that they are a very physical front seven.
Meyers has also missed practice time with an ankle injury that has limited him. He will be key to the offense’s success as one more weapon who allows Lawrence to spread the ball around. If he’s hindered in any way, it could affect the offense, especially in the passing game.
Starting center Robert Hainsey is also not expected to play because of a sprained knee suffered in last week’s win over Tennessee.
The Giants’ initial goal should be to shut down the Jaguars’ rushing attack and make them one-dimensional.
Yes, Lawrence has been good as a passer this season, but he is not without fault. Making him consistently do the right thing as a passer has a higher probability of success than trying to figure out on a play-by-play basis whether the Jaguars are running or passing.
Look for high-low brackets on Washington, because he is their most explosive element as a receiver. And look for the Giants’ offense to really work Hunter, since if he has his hands full playing cornerback, it’s hard for him to help on the offensive side of the ball.
Ultimately, success could hinge on the team’s ability to pressure Lawrence and turn him into a scrambler, where he’s prone to mistakes.

title: Giants Rookie Malachi Fields Is Quietly Making His Case for a Bigger Role
full_text:
New York Giants rookie receiver Malachi Fields has been an afterthought in an offense that has primarily featured tight end Isaiah Likely and receiver Malik Nabers as its main pass targets.
But of late, Fields, for whom the Giants traded back into the third round of the 2026 draft so they could select him out of Notre Dame, has been quietly making a case for a bigger piece of the pie.
The 6-foot-4, 222-pound Fields has caught 22 of 38 targets for 350 yards and one touchdown. Of that yardage, 108 yards have come after the catch, and he has also proven to be a sure-handed receiver who has yet to drop a pass.
“Not surprised at all with him,” said offensive coordinator Matt Nagy. “You all have heard me talk about him all camp. His ceiling — when we have this conversation five years from now, you’re going to think about this question you’re asking me because he’s really good.”
Nabers agreed with Nagy’s assessment.
“Just giving him the ball in space, I think he gets open pretty well,” he said. “I think he has good feet for how tall he is; he runs fast, can track the ball well.
“He gets in and out of his breaks. We’ve been seeing it on film, so I’m happy we’re giving him more opportunities to get into a rhythm and get him more plays.”
Not only has Fields been solid as a receiver, but his physicality has also shown up on tape as a downfield blocker for the running game. So one would think an expanded role might be on deck for the 23-year-old, right?
Maybe not just yet, but it’s certainly not going to be because of Fields’ performance.
“When you look at Malachi, he’s catching the football, which is your number one job as a receiver, and also making blocks and then making plays when he’s supposed to,” said Nagy.
“He’s got great talent. He does everything right. And I think that ceiling is just going to continue to get higher and higher.”
Nabers added, “As young as he is coming into this league, he’s making the most of every chance that he gets, every opportunity, so he’ll get more for sure.”

title: Matt Nagy’s Accountability Shows Harbaugh’s Giants Culture at Work
full_text:
In the old days, whatever a coach or any authority figure, for that matter, said, that’s what went, right or wrong.
That was especially true in sports, where an athlete on a team struggling to win games, in response to a question about the play-calling the coach was asking of the team, said, “Every play is designed to work.”
In the world of John Harbaugh and the New York Giants locker room, that is certainly true. Every play the coaches put into a weekly game plan is indeed designed to work. However, the difference is that every play called is designed to work only if called at the right moment.
Accountability. It’s a running theme in the Giants locker room these days under Harbaugh.
And it includes the coaches just as much as the players — look at offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, who on Thursday admitted that his play-call decision on what turned out to be a failed third-and-3 quarterback run by J.J. McCarthy that lost 2 yards at the two-minute mark in last week’s 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders left him “pissed.”
Rightfully so. After the Giants punted, the Commanders drove downfield before throwing the ultimate gut punt at their division rivals by snatching the win — and the head-to-head tiebreaker — from the NFC East-leading Giants.
Nagy didn’t just admit it publicly. He said he made it “very clear” to the players that he dropped the ball.
“That's important for them to know,” he said of his admission. “If you can't take accountability or accept responsibility in this process, you'll never gain respect and trust from your peers. And I wouldn't say that to you if I didn't believe it. But I'd also be an idiot, a fool, not an idiot, but a fool if I didn't learn from it.”
The admission was welcomed by the players, including receiver Malik Nabers, who seemed willing to forgive the coach’s screw-up.
“He's seen us run that play in practice, and he felt really good about it, but it comes down to, as players, we've got to execute the play call that's being called,” Nabers said. “No matter what in that game, we've got to do exactly what we have to do to get the first down. That's all we needed, and we'll do better next time.”
While Nagy might appreciate the understanding he received from guys like his star receiver, that hasn’t dimmed his quest to be a better play caller.
“I need to be able to learn from it, use that as a play caller, let those guys see it, feel it, and trust it,” he said.
“And then when the play is called, they believe in it, and then they make it happen. And we have a better success story than what we did last week.”

title: Giants Dennard Wilson Says LB Abdul Carter is Just Getting Started
full_text:
If the New York Giants earn a Week 11 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars at MetLife Stadium, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson believes linebacker Abdul Carter must play an integral role in the defensive game plan.
The No. 3 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft has been one of the Giants’ most important defenders this season. Carter has made nine starts and compiled 22 total tackles (three for loss), eight quarterback hits, two sacks, and one forced fumble.
Though his sack total has drawn some criticism, Wilson said the 23-year-old is playing at a high level.
“I think he’s played extremely well. If you watch him, he’s been extremely disruptive,” Wilson said Thursday.
“He’s making a lot of plays. The sack numbers aren’t there, but he’s affecting the game. A lot of holding calls, a lot of pressures. He’s getting the quarterback off the spot so that the sacks will come.
"We’re trying to put him in positions for him to get some touches on the quarterback, but he’s doing everything he’s supposed to do.”
Under Wilson, the Giants have adopted a pass-rush style built on blitz pressure. The unit has been much more effective with schemed pressures, thanks to Carter and fellow linebackers Kayvon Thibodeaux and Arvell Reese.
To find success Sunday, Wilson said the defense must do a better job of converting pressure, even as others may find more opportunities to take down Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence.
“We all need to do a better job of converting, especially on play-action pass on non-3rd down situations, non-pass situations. And just as a whole, as a collective, as you rush better together, they’ll have to move away from him at times if somebody else is hitting the quarterback. But I think it’s all going to come.”
What Carter lacks in sacks, he makes up for with pressure. PFF has credited the Penn State product with 28 pressures, including 20 quarterback hurries, this season.
With Lawrence ranking sixth in passing grade against the blitz, Carter’s production could swing the game.
After all, few pass rushers in the NFL combine speed and power the way Carter does. His athleticism and instincts give him the chance to be a consistent, disruptive force against opposing quarterbacks, only increasing his value to New York’s defense.
According to Wilson, the young pass rusher is just getting started.
“One thing about Abdul is this: he has high expectations,” Wilson said. “He’s doing his job to the best of his ability. And other things will happen for him. Man, you should see the guy. He works so hard in the meeting rooms, trying to understand the game plan, and he takes pride in being a disciplined football player.
“And he’s still progressing,” he added. “You look at him from last year to this year and how he’s playing, how dependable he is, how accountable he is. He’s doing the little things correctly.
“Everything else is going to take care of itself because he has that dynamic ability and that dynamic trait. It will turn on. And when it turns on, watch out.”

title: Jets Continue to Be Sneaky Winners of Colts' Failed Daniel Jones' Experiment
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are the gift that keeps on giving the whole year for the New York Jets.
When Indianapolis acquired Sauce Gardner in a trade for two first-round picks, the belief from the organization was that the All-Pro cornerback was the missing piece to the organization ending their playoff drought. Since that trade, though, the Colts are just 4-15.
And every move they have made since is a massive win for the Jets. That includes their most recent decision to release quarterback Daniel Jones after not trading him at the NFL Trade Deadline last week.
New York may be 2-8, but its future outlook is far different than that of Indianapolis. They own three first-round picks in the 2027 draft, with two projected to be in the top five as of this current moment.
Indianapolis had a chance this deadline to help themselves in that regard. They traded away All-Pro players like DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson. Josh Downs and Keenan Allen were also moved for mid-round selections.
Despite the firesale, the Colts chose to keep running back Jonathan Taylor and Jones on the roster, believing they could still compete with them beyond this season.
The decision to release Jones and roll with former top pick Anthony Richardson as quarterback is a sign the Colts simply did not have a plan for the trade deadline this year. They looked at players with expiring contracts and simply sold them off for a mediocre return. They overvalued other players like Jones and Taylor for no other reason, but they didn't receive the offer they want.
Part of that is due to the team firing general manager Chris Ballard before the deadline. Interim GM Ed Dodds is having to try and prove his worthiness at the top job, while also not hurting long-term assets for the franchise.
But the circus of Jones' release just a week after the deadline so the Colts get nothing for him is an abject failure by the front office.
And the Jets are looking on like that meme of Bill Hader eating popcorn on Saturday Night Live .
New York has had to do nothing but allow the Colts to collapse inward. The acquisition of Gardner gave the Jets two first-round picks that they are using to rebuild their struggling roster. Indianapolis, meanwhile, has no first-round pick to use to rebuild theirs.
The release of Jones is just the latest example of the difference between the two teams as well. New York has had no illusions about their current poor roster, so they got a king's ransom for one of their more talented players . The Colts, meanwhile, hitched their wagon to Jones in the hopes they could build a winner immediately.
And as each week passes by, and both teams continue to lose, it's the Jets who should come out as the better team with both picks expected to be in the top five.

title: 3 Positions the Jets Must Target in Round 1 of the 2027 NFL Draft
full_text:
Barring any unforeseen circumstances, the Jets are going to walk into the 2027 NFL Draft with three first-round picks that will be considered within reach of impact players.
The question becomes which positions and players the team should focus on. It's easy to point to the current 2-8 team and argue they have holes all over the roster, but that is not always the case. In fact, the Jets are better prepared to take the next steps in the rebuild than in any other year before.
The question simply becomes: which area of need should the team focus on? And in that regard, there are three that are more important than all the others.
A team doesn't have three first-round picks in a draft if they don't intend to take a quarterback early. The 2022 Jets are the exception, not the rule.
This time, though, it seems like a foregone conclusion that the team will be focusing on a signal-caller early in the draft, despite past whiffs at the position elsewhere . While there are still decisions that have to be made by many of the quarterbacks in the draft, the safe bet is that three college players will make the jump to the NFL.
Mestemaker is the quarterback with the highest ceiling. He has the athleticism and arm talent of a Josh Allen, which would excite any team. Carr is a more traditional pocket passer who can make all NFL throws. Mensah is a quarterback who has a mix of both Carr and Mestemaker, but may be a bit of a lesser player at each. This isn't to say the Miami quarterback is bad—I firmly expect all three to go into the top 10 of this draft.
And that means New York will come away with one of them.
David Bailey is a rising star in the league, but New York still has major questions at edge rusher. Who they end up selecting will largely be based on who is running the defense in 2027 . If a coordinator wants to run more of a 4-3 scheme, then the Jets would want players who can operate out of the wide nine.
A 3-4 scheme, meanwhile, required edge rushers to be stout against the run as well as the pass. Luckily for New York, the top edge prospects they'll be in line for can handle both. Stewart and Simmons have dominated college football this season. They remain favorites for top-five picks depending on how the draft lines up.
As things stand, the Jets are set to get their future QB and an impact edge defender. That's an excellent haul to rebuild a roster.
It's not just at edge rusher where New York needs major help. Their inability to target an every-down defensive tackle following the Quinnen Williams trade is also a major problem. Luckily for the Jets, many interior defensive linemen are available.
Echoles and Gilliam are two players who could be available when New York makes its third selection in the draft. Both have shown the ability to rush the passer and defend the run at a high clip. It offers New York a chance to solidify the defensive line in a major way very early on draft day.

title: 3 Key Jets vs. Chargers Matchups That Will Decide If New York Tastes Victory in Week 11
full_text:
After extending their losing streak to five games last Sunday, the Jets will look to get back into the win column when they head out west to take on the Chargers at SoFi Stadium. Unlike New York’s last two matchups, which came against two of the AFC’s premier teams, Los Angeles has arguably been the worst team this season.
While the Chargers' defense has been average this season, offensive struggles and mounting injuries have derailed their season. For head coach Aaron Glenn, a win here could go a long way toward cooling his hot seat ; however, a loss against Los Angeles would effectively cement his firing.
If the Jets are going to come away victorious, they must prioritize winning these three key matchups.
While some point to the schematic shift or lack of talent for the Chargers’ offensive struggles, injuries upfront have played a large part. Los Angeles currently has five offensive linemen on injured reserve, four of whom played in the interior.
As a result, the Chargers have relied on two rookies in the middle, along with five-year veteran Cole Strange at right guard. While Logan Taylor has done well in pass protection this season, allowing just two sacks and seven pressures across 212 pass-blocking snaps, the same can’t be said for Slaughter and Strange.
Slaughter has surrendered two sacks and 14 pressures, earning a 60.1 pass-blocking grade, which ranks 22nd among 35 qualifying centers , per Pro Football Focus. Meanwhile, Strange has given up three sacks and 23 pressures. His 37.7 pass-blocking grade ranks 70th among 77 qualifying guards, per PFF.
With Los Angeles vulnerable in the middle, New York must target this area in Sunday’s matchup. While the Jets aren’t among the league’s best at generating pressure, they’ve had some success getting to the backfield this season. Through 10 games, they are tied for 13th in sacks (23) and rank 16th in pressure rate (23.1%).
David Bailey has played a major role in the pass rush, leading the team in sacks (7.5) and quarterback hits (12). While Bailey and Will McDonald IV have been New York’s top pass rushers, the defense hasn’t been able to get much pressure up the middle. Interior defenders account for just three of the team’s 23 sacks, with Jowon Briggs having two of them.
David Bailey had both Patrick Mahomes and Kenneth Walker BEGGING for mercy. Bailey now has 7.5 sacks (T-3rd in NFL) and 5 FF’s (1st in NFL) on his rookie season. The Jets seem to have found their franchise pass rusher in the rookie OLB 😳🔥 pic.twitter.com/Dp0cBc2vzx
For the Jets to increase their chances of winning, they’ll need to exploit the Chargers' weak interior and send pressure up the middle. New York ranks fifth in blitz rate (33.8%), and a more aggressive approach from its linebackers could help take advantage of Los Angeles’ protection woes.
The Jets must use Demario Davis on interior blitzes, as he has already recorded two sacks doing so this season. Jamien Sherwood should also be used in similar situations, as he has the speed and athleticism to get to the quarterback.
This would give the Jets another way to create pressure without relying solely on their edge rushers.
With Geno Smith expected to play Sunday, he’s poised to bounce back against the Chargers. Los Angeles’ secondary has been subpar this season, ranking 23rd in passing yards allowed per game (233.4) and tied for 11th in passing touchdowns allowed (13). Its heavy reliance on zone could also work in Smith’s favor.
According to Sharp Football Analysis, the Chargers rank 23rd in zone rate (23.9%) and are in man coverage just 13.4% of the time. This is an encouraging sign for Smith, as the 14-year veteran has feasted against zone coverage this season, completing 71.3% of his passes for eight yards per attempt.
However, Smith has been criticized for playing too conservatively this season, as he tends to take his time in the pocket while searching for an opening downfield. While that patience has occasionally worked against him, as it’s contributed to his 29 sacks this season (third-most in the NFL), he’s at his best when he has time to read and dissect the defense.
That’s where the Chargers’ reliance on zone coverage could work in his favor. Zone defenses allow Smith to identify soft spots in the secondary and find open receivers. Rather than forcing throws into tight windows, he can use his patience to find receivers in space. Fortunately for Smith, the Jets’ offensive line has done a good job of giving him time, as he ranks ninth in average time to throw (2.93) , per NFL Next Gen Stats.
While the Chargers could certainly look to switch things up against Smith and play more man coverage, their secondary injuries could limit any potential changes. Derwin James is already on the injured reserve, while Rodney Shelley missed Wednesday and Thursday’s practices. Kendall Williamson also missed Thursday’s practice, while Donte Jackson and Isas Waxter were limited participants.
With limited depth in their back end, the Chargers will likely stick to what’s worked for them and try to confuse Smith at the line of scrimmage with blitz disguises and simulated pressure. This could play right into Smith’s strengths, especially if the offensive line can continue to provide him enough time.
When Mike McDaniel became the new offensive coordinator for the Chargers, many thought that he would raise the unit’s play and help elevate Justin Herbert to the upper echelon of quarterbacks. However, Los Angeles’ transition to McDaniel’s offense has done more harm than good.
Herbert has regressed significantly in the new system, consistently making costly mistakes, and the offense has struggled to put up points. The unit hasn’t lived up to expectations and ranks near the bottom in every major statistical category except rushing.
Despite several injuries upfront, the Chargers’ rushing attack has had some success this season, ranking 11th in rushing yards per game (119.6) and tied for 13th in rushing yards per attempt (4.2). Los Angeles is coming off its best rushing performance of the season, thanks to Omarion Hampton, who rushed for 105 of the team’s 160 yards and a touchdown in the team’s Monday night win against the Ravens.
McDaniel finally gave the second-year back from North Carolina the majority of the workload after leaning on a three-back rotation for much of the season. Since that approach led to a win, the Chargers will likely continue to use Hampton as a feature back against the Jets.
New York has notoriously struggled to contain the run this season, ranking 30th in rushing yards allowed per game (135.3), tied for the fourth-most rushing touchdowns allowed, and tied for the third-most rushes of 10+ yards allowed. The unit also hasn’t allowed fewer than 90 rushing yards since Week 2.
Given the Jets' struggles against the run, the team must prioritize holding Hampton in check. He’s a physical, downhill runner who’s also fast for his size, running a 4.46-second 40-yard dash at the NFL Scouting Combine.
Although his numbers don’t back it up this season, he excels at creating extra yards after contact. Hampton averaged 3.95 yards after contact against the Ravens and is tied for 27th in yards after contact per attempt (2.95) , per PFF.
Winning at the point of attack and getting to Hampton before he can build up any momentum will be critical for New York, as slowing Hampton down will force Los Angeles into more passing situations and shut down play-action opportunities.
The Jets have struggled against play-action this season, allowing a 67% completion rate and 8.1 yards per attempt , according to Sharp Football Analysis. With Herbert ranking 12th in play-action dropback rate (26.9%), New York must limit Hampton’s success on the ground and force the Chargers to beat them through the air.
If New York contains Hampton, it’ll significantly increase its chances of winning.

title: Kenyon Sadiq Can't Be a Jets Afterthought Any Longer as Week 11 Injury Report Remains Grim
full_text:
The Jets are in the midst of what appears to be another lost season in Gotham following a 31-12 loss to the Bills last Sunday, a game they were competitive in for a half until the decision to settle for field goals eventually caught up with them.
While a trip out west to face a 1-8 Chargers team that ranks last in the league in scoring offense (16 ppg) would seem like a favorable opportunity at first glance, it is not as simple as that due to a coaching staff that can't seem to get out of its own way this season with its inability to get the ball to its best players.
Wide receiver Garrett Wilson may be the first name who comes to mind, but someone else offensive coordinator Frank Reich has failed to distribute the ball to consistently has been rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq, which is just another reason why the OC is officially on the clock to save his job with a Week 13 bye looming .
Sadiq has certainly not been used as often as fans wanted, but there is no reason he should be an afterthought going into Sunday's game. After confirming that WRs Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle, hip) and Isaiah Williams (ribs) have been ruled out, ESPN 's Rich Cimini noted on Friday that Wilson, Adonai Mitchell, Tim Patrick and Malik McClain are the only four healthy wideouts the Jets will have, while also mentioning that "Sterling Shepard could come up from the practice squad."
Jets are down to 4 healthy WRs - Wilson, Mitchell, Tim Patrick and Malik McClain. Sterling Shepard could come up from the practice squad. Glenn says TEs Sadiq and Taylor give them WR-type players in multi-TE packages. https://t.co/G40oCb9Vuw
Head coach Aaron Glenn pointed out Sadiq and fellow TE Mason Taylor as players who "give them WR-type players in multi-TE packages," so it is even more important that the Jets keep their word and start using the rookie TE more as a receiver, especially with Cooper and Williams ruled out.
The Jets already had a concerning injury report earlier in the week , and now that the status of some of those players is being determined, it is even more obvious that Sadiq needs to be a bigger factor in this offense. There is no question about the plethora of weapons the Jets have to get the ball to, but the rookie has the athleticism and speed to provide a spark to an offense that has gone the last nine quarters without scoring a touchdown.
After all, Sadiq burst onto the scene with a rushing TD in the season opener before going off for seven catches (on eight targets), 105 yards and a TD in the Week 3 loss to the Lions. That said, he has only two multi-reception games since then while being targeted four times or fewer in those games. Aside from his four catches for 49 yards against the Chiefs in Week 9, Sadiq has had 22 receiving yards or fewer in every other game since that Week 3 breakout.
From the other capable players surrounding him in the pass attack to the coaching malpractice, Sadiq's quiet stretch raises several questions about the Jets . While he could potentially be one of the biggest winners to emerge if a trade for Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell were to come to fruition as Glenn's tenure in Gotham nears its end, there is no reason for him to remain an afterthought right now if the Jets use the mounting injuries as an opportunity.
Aside from Wilson and Mitchell, who have a combined four receiving TDs, Taylor (two) and TE Jeremy Ruckert (one) are the only other healthy players on this roster besides Sadiq who have found the end zone. The current quarterback conundrum is not ideal , as Geno Smith battles through a left ankle injury and rookie Cade Klubnik continues to adjust to the NFL, but a 23rd-ranked Chargers pass defense (233.4 ypg) could be just what the doctor ordered for Sadiq and this Jets offense to get back on track.
Sadiq has certainly not been utilized as you would expect from a player who was drafted as the 16th overall pick with so much upside. However, Glenn has made it clear that Sadiq and Taylor could be used as WRs with Cooper and Williams out of the lineup.
Now, it's time for him and Reich to back that up and find a way to get Sadiq more involved in the Jets' offense as the injuries continue to pile up.

title: 4 Upcoming Jets UFAs on Track to Be Shown the Door This Offseason
full_text:
Sitting at 2-8 at the midpoint of the season, the Jets are on the verge of missing the playoffs for the 16th consecutive season.
There are several reasons you can point to for New York’s failures this season, including injuries, questionable coaching decisions, and poor execution by the players. Ultimately, this iteration of the team just hasn’t played winning football, and as a result, another coaching turnover will likely occur.
If this is the case, they will also overhaul the roster in the offseason and add some fresh faces to the mix. Although it’s still too early to determine, here are four upcoming Jets free agents the team shouldn't bring back.
Despite making little to no contributions during his first two years, Braiden McGregor somehow made the Jets’ final roster once again. To everyone’s surprise, it finally looked like he was showing some real progression in the team’s Week 1 win against the Titans.
The former Michigan Wolverine finished with three total tackles and played a key role in helping New York hold Tennessee to just 68 rushing yards, earning a 77.2 run-defense grade , per Pro Football Focus .
Despite this, McGregor was unable to provide a similar impact before his season was cut short after suffering a torn pectoral muscle in the team’s Week 4 loss to the Bears. Although the former 2024 undrafted free agent displayed some flashes in Week 1, he just hasn’t provided enough production to warrant another contract.
Through 23 career games, he’s recorded just 28 total tackles, one sack, and 11 pressures. He’s shown little progress as an edge rusher, and he hasn't proven to be a quality depth contributor. In his absence, Nate Lynn has established himself as the better option, registering five total tackles and a sack in just 51 defensive snaps.
Given his lack of development and limited production, New York shouldn’t re-sign McGregor.
Before the season, Kene Nwangwu was widely considered to be an instrumental piece of the Jets despite not having a role on offense. Over his six-year career, Nwangwu has established himself as one of the premier kick returners, averaging 28.8 yards per return and returning five kicks for a touchdown.
Last year, Nwangwu led all qualifying returners in yards per return (33.6) and was one of five players to return a kick for a touchdown , per PFF . However, the former Iowa State Cyclone has taken a significant step back this season.
Through six games, Nwangwu has returned 16 kicks for an average of 24 yards per return, which is the lowest average of his career. Although a back and knee injury have hampered him this year, Nwangwu clearly doesn’t have the same explosiveness he once did.
While having a dynamic returner on special teams is a game-changer, his limited production and injury history should give New York enough reason to move on.
The Jets weren’t expecting Tim Patrick to be one of their top receivers this season. Instead, they hoped the nine-year veteran could mentor the younger receivers and play a key role in the run game as a blocker.
That hasn’t been the case. Although a groin injury forced him to miss the first four games, Patrick returned for the team’s Week 5 matchup against the Browns, where he recorded two receptions for 26 yards.
Since then, Patrick has appeared in just two games, recording one reception for 15 yards, and has been a healthy scratch. A big reason Patrick has been inactive these last few weeks is that he simply hasn’t been much of a factor.
About to turn 33 on Monday, Patrick has displayed regression as a blocker and receiver and has done more harm than good for New York. He’s committed two costly penalties this season—one of which negated an Omar Cooper Jr. touchdown on the opening drive, stifling the momentum the Jets’ offense had leading up to the play.
With this, it’s best if both sides move on in the offseason.
Since being traded to New York days before the start of the 2025 season, Harrison Phillips quickly emerged as one of the team's locker room leaders. While the nine-year veteran has been a great locker room guy, his production has declined significantly this season.
Through 10 games, Phillips has registered 36 total tackles, 10 of which came in a single game, eight pressures, and 17 stops. His play, particularly against the run, has not been up to his standard.
Last year, Phillips earned a 76.4 run-defense grade , per PFF , which ranked sixth among 134 qualifying interior defenders. Meanwhile, this season, Phillips has a 57.1 run-defense grade, the second-lowest mark of his career.
With his play declining and New York giving Darrell Jackson Jr. and Jack Heflin more opportunities, there just isn’t room for Phillips anymore.

title: Faria: Jets' End-of-Year Plans to Tank (or Not) Likely Won't Make a Difference
full_text:
It is as if Shakespeare has taken over the NFL now that the playoff picture is becoming clearer.
To tank or not to tank? That is the question.
For the Jets, the team won't even accept the question for the remainder of the season. Despite their 2-8 start to the year , Gang Green has focused heavily on trying to win as many games as possible down the stretch.
"I don't think anybody in this business is here to lose," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "I don't think anybody in this business can stomach just going out there and trying to lose; that's just not the way that we're built... regardless of the record."
Glenn and the players may believe in focusing on winning games, but is that the best thing for the franchise in the long run? What benefits does trying to win games down the stretch bring to the Jets and to a head coach who is seemingly in the hot seat ?
What if I told you none of it really matters—including the team's decision to not tank in the first place.
Jets fans may want the team to try to lose, but that's just not the reality of what the organization is going to do. That is the danger of trying to do everything in their power to keep their coaching staff forto a third season at the helm. The focus isn't on the future success of the organization; it's about the immediate success.
In fact, very few cases in NFL history show teams actually tanking. Most bad teams are simply bad enough to lose and get high picks—especially with seven games left in the season. For Jets fans to want the team to tank, that is simply not what they are going to do.
However, it might not actually matter.
The Jets' coaching staff has struggled all season. It hasn't mattered whether it's against top competition like the Chiefs or against the one-win Dolphins. The Jets seemingly can't get out of their own way when it comes to winning games.
Because of that reality, who is to say the team needs to tank in order to get a top pick?
New York is seventh-worst in the league in points, 10th-worst in points allowed, and third-worst against the run. As of Week 11, the Jets haven't scored a touchdown in nine quarters, thanks to their coaching staff being comfortable with kicking field goals after failed red zone attempts. The talent increase seen across the roster hasn't mattered. The upgrade at quarterback hasn't mattered.
So what will suddenly be fixed down the stretch? Will those numbers magically improve against the Chargers or the Dolphins?
It's fair for fans to want the team to lose games down the stretch in order to secure a top draft pick in April, but that's not what the organization is going to set out to do at this point.
With how poorly they have played this season, making an effort to tank may not matter at all.

title: Potential Kevin O'Connell Trade Would Be a Colossal Jets Mistake Waiting to Happen
full_text:
As the Jets look to turn the page from an injury-riddled 31-12 loss to the Bills last Sunday and try to get their season back on track amid a five-game losing streak, there are still a lot of areas of concern that need to be improved on ahead of a Week 11 road trip to face the 1-8 Chargers.
While New York's upcoming opponents, the Chargers and Dolphins, have a combined 2-16 record and should present some favorable opportunities before a Week 13 bye, the problems on this team run much deeper than the surface , especially for head coach Aaron Glenn.
With a 5-22 record as Jets HC and a dismal 0-9 mark against AFC East opponents, Glenn has failed to get it done in Gotham and it should only be a matter of time until Gang Green decides to move on . Although there are multiple ways for the Jets to go for their next HC when that time comes, ESPN 's Rich Cimini suggested that Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell could be a "name to watch."
"The name I would watch for is KOC, Kevin O'Connell," Cimini said (h/t Jets Collective). "I was just talking to a couple of people in the league today, and they said they could see (Jets general manager Darren) Mougey giving up a high draft pick for Kevin O'Connell. They went to college together; they have maintained a relationship. If something falls apart there in Minnesota, if they collapse down the stretch, or if they decide that they want to elevate (Vikings defensive coordinator Brian) Flores instead of losing him to another team, maybe they make that move."
. @RichCimini said the "name to watch" for the #Jets in the 2027 search is #Vikings HC Kevin O'Connell. “The name I would watch for is KOC, Kevin O’Connell. I was just talking to a couple of people in the league today, and they said they could see [Darren] Mougey giving up a high… pic.twitter.com/i1wNAcrG8p
While O'Connell has a solid 50-27 record (.649) as a HC and has long been heralded as a quarterback whisperer, he is still 0-2 in the playoffs and may be someone the Jets want to consider carefully.
After all, with three first-round draft picks, they could land a top-five talent at QB amid the injury concerns that starter Geno Smith is currently facing , and you could argue it would be much more valuable to keep those picks instead of giving up one to land O'Connell.
Sure, this is a team that has dealt with its fair share of injuries throughout the season and has struggled to remain at full strength, but that is still no excuse for the lack of adjustments and conservative approach that continue to plague Glenn on the sidelines, with New York's season continuing to unravel.
You cannot argue with the talent spread throughout the Jets' depth chart, but this is still a roster that is far from complete and one that can certainly benefit from a trio of first-round picks if used correctly on the right players.
For starters, the defense has been a mess all season, particularly its third-worst run defense (135.3 ypg) and repeated struggles from the linebackers . Additionally, the offense has struggled to convert third downs and ranks last in red-zone efficiency (37.9%), some obvious signs that change should be on the way at some point in the immediate future.
With an NFC North title in 2022 and a much better overall record, there is no doubt that O'Connell would be an upgrade over Glenn. At the same time, is he really worth the Jets giving up a first-round pick for?
With an unproven track record in the playoffs and, most recently, a disappointing 2025 season that culminated in the Vikings missing the playoffs altogether with a 9-8 record, that is certainly debatable.
Until the Vikings reunited with QB Kirk Cousins at the trade deadline and came away with a 30-10 win over the Packers last Sunday—only their second game with at least 30 points this season—the Vikings struggled at QB and had to rely on their top-ranked defense (14 ppg) to do the heavy lifting. O'Connell put his faith in Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz, only for neither to be the answer.
There was also the J.J. McCarthy saga: the 2024 first-rounder battled numerous injuries and accounted for more interceptions (12) than passing TDs (11) during his second season before getting traded to the Giants.
Considering the conundrum the Jets currently face at QB with the uncertainty facing Smith and the timidness that rookie Cade Klubnik showed in his first regular-season appearance against the Bills, it is fair to question if they want a similar situation to the one that transpired with McCarthy and the Vikings when searching for their franchise QB.
At this point, there is still plenty of time for Klubnik to continue to develop and for Smith to potentially lead this team to some wins if he can stay healthy, but it is also time to start looking ahead and get a feel for what the future might hold in Gotham.
With multiple coaches finding themselves in hot water to begin Week 11 and questions surrounding overall execution on the field, there will definitely be changes in store.
The upside is there with O'Connell, especially compared to Glenn's disastrous tenure with the Jets. However, the former's lack of postseason success and recent QB struggles make this a risky trade that may not be worth it for a Jets team that has a lot of draft capital.

title: 5 Things Darren Mougey Has Done Right to Fix Jets in 2026 and Beyond
full_text:
It's easy to look at the current record of the New York Jets and declare that head coach Aaron Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey are a package deal. After all, their 5-22 record together is among the worst in team history.
But context must be included when talking about the Jets' current structure. Glenn was hired before Mougey, and while the roster has improved greatly, the coaching has not . At this moment, it's easy to see a path to New York keeping Mougey past 2026 and moving on from Glenn entirely.
If that were to happen, New York needs to look only at five decisions from Mougey that have proven to be right for the franchise's future.
Sometimes an extension for a productive player on a bad roster isn't in the best interest of the organization. Mougey understands that well - it's one of the reasons why two of his replacements this year have been such massive upgrades.
Mougey upgraded at left guard and kicker this offseason. Offensively, the team let John Simpson walk in free agency, believing they could find someone cheaper and better than the veteran guard. Dylan Parham was signed to a two-year deal to be his replacement. All he has done is become the sixth-best guard in football. Simpson, meanwhile, has been average at best.
The same could be said at kicker. Nick Folk had an excellent season in 2025, but New York let him walk to Atlanta. After a position battle, the team found Jason Sanders, and the former All-Pro has gone 25-for-28 on field goals. Meanwhile, the Falcons released Folk.
Understanding when to let good players go is important for a quality general manager. Replacing those players with upgrades is even more important. And that's what Mougey has done this season alone.
Geno Smith is incredibly important to the Jets, not just for the 2026 season, but beyond that as well. New York needs a veteran quarterback they can rely on not only to bridge the gap to a future rookie, but also to be someone capable of playing good football and leading by example.
The best plan for the Jets is to draft a quarterback and have him set behind Smith for the 2027 season. This is the same plan the Kansas City Chiefs ran with Patrick Mahomes when he was made a first-round pick in 2017. Other examples like Tom Brady, Carson Palmer, Drew Brees, Phillip Rivers,  and Eli Manning also fit the idea of the Jets pairing Smith with a rookie signal-caller.
Until the Jets draft a quarterback who can win them games, the team will continue to struggle. The good news is that their current plan for the room is the one that has been tried and tested to be successful. And Mougey should be commended for it.
How he takes the rookie quarterback, and if that player develops, will be the next stage of that process.
The worst mistake New York could have made this season would have been going overboard to surround the current coaching staff with weapons. Trading 2027 or 2028 draft capital at the deadline to bolster the current team would not have changed their outlook this season. It wouldn't have saved Glenn, nor would it have altered the team's current 2-8 record.
Mougey has done a good job of understanding where the roster is. Last season, they were bad enough that acquiring draft capital for the likes of Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner would help the team's future.
This year, the team improved its talent and understood that the best way to build toward 2026 was to add it with draft picks, not with deadline acquisitions. Unlike the team's head coach, the Jets have a general manager with a modern plan who gets what needs to happen to get there.
It's important for teams to find value across the roster. One thing that the Jets have actually done well is finding players that many wouldn't expect to fill needs, and doing so at a very reasonable price.
This season has been a good example of that. New York signed edge rusher Kingsley Enagbare to a one-year deal worth just $10 million. Safety Dane Belton signed another one-year deal worth $4 million. Other free-agent pickups like Dylan Parham have also been a quality value.
However, Mougey's free agent history isn't a perfect run . Misses on Demario Davis, Justin Fields, and Joseph Ossai haven't helped the team as much as many would have hoped. That said, New York's goal is to improve the current roster. Unequivocally, the Jets have done it, and it is due to Mougey understanding areas of need and market value for each.
No general manager is above mistakes. Even the elites make them over the course of their career.
Great general managers, though, don't let their mistakes become long-term issues. The San Francisco 49ers whiffed on Trey Lance in 2021, but responded by drafting Brock Purdy. That first-round mistake, therefore, isn't as bad as it could have been.
The good thing Mougey has done is not make long-term mistakes. Many of the draft picks that have yet to pan out for the team are late-round selections. No GM is going to get fired over that. Even free agent signings that have failed do not put the Jets in a hole in terms of dead cap or future spending.
Mougey hasn't been perfect with the Jets. But he hasn't made the crippling mistakes that other executives have made with the team. For Joe Douglas, it was selecting Zach Wilson, trading for Haason Reddick, and whiffing on the offensive line.
Mougey hasn't gotten to that point yet. And therefore should get more chances moving forward.

title: Jets Shed Light on Their D'Angelo Ponds Feelings After Quiet Week 10
full_text:
Do the New York Jets have a plan for slot cornerback D'Angelo Ponds? The second-round pick received his second start of the season last week against Buffalo, but only played seven snaps.
Part of that decision came down to their opponent. Buffalo ran wild on New York to the tune of over 200 yards in a 31-12 blowout. Because of Buffalo's rushing success, the Jets opted to play former mid-round pick Malachi Moore four times as many snaps as Ponds.
That doesn't mean the the rookie played poorly, though.
Speaking to reporters in his new role as defensive play-caller, coordinator Brian Duker gave the Indiana prospect a major vote of confidence going into their next showdown against the Los Angeles Chargers.
Duker was clear. Despite playing only seven snaps in the team's loss, Ponds put forth the kind of game that the team was looking for over the last few weeks.
"I thought he did a nice job, probably his best game yet this past weekend," Duker said. "I thought his execution was the cleanest, that's probably the best way to say it. His executions of his assignment, where he was supposed to be, leverages, all those types of things."
So if the team believed that Ponds played well on Sunday, then why exactly did they play him significantly less than Moore?
The answer to that is New York's failing on defense. The Jets' front seven has been gutted consistently due to injuries and their focus on playing four downlinemen has put them in situations they can't stop at this point. By adding a bigger player in Moore, the team hopes a third safety will be better than adding a third cornerback on the field.
It's a sign that the team still needs to see more from Ponds in run defense as well.
With the Jets sitting at 2-8, there should be little the team needs to see more of from the safety room. It would be best for the team to play Ponds as much as possible to determine what kind of player he can be. Can he handle being a boundary corner despite his size? Is he just a slot player?
These are questions that can't be answered yet. By season's end, they must have one. New York has done a poor job of putting young players in the best positions possible. Ponds has been a good example of this. He hasn't been given enough of an opportunity to really know what kind of performer he can be.
But if they are to improve beyond 2027, the team will need to actually play them. If Ponds had the "best game" of his young career, then he will need more playing time altogether.

title: 3 Jets Would Be the Winners of a Potential Kevin O’Connell Trade
full_text:
The New York Jets have reached the point in the season where fans and media are speculating about a new head coach. New York holds a 2-8 record through 10 weeks, and every loss seems to be another nail in Aaron Glenn’s head-coaching coffin .
ESPN's Rich Cimini threw out Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell as a surprise candidate on the Jets Collective podcast (h/t UStadium) as speculation continues over who will be the Jets' next head coach.
New York would have to make a trade for the Vikings' head coach, with O’Connell still under contract in Minnesota, but the coach would immediately impact the team. The fifth-year head coach has a 50-27 record and has fielded at least a seven-win team every year during his tenure. If New York traded for the head coach, these three Jets would immediately benefit from Kevin O’Connell’s arrival.
Wilson would arguably benefit most from the Jets trading for the Vikings’ head coach. O’Connell has experience with a top-five receiver in Justin Jefferson. That experience would do wonders in unlocking the 26-year-old. Wilson has shown he has the talent to be a top receiver in the NFL; O’Connell could be the one to elevate the Jet to that level.
Justin Jefferson has averaged 9.24 targets per game during O’Connell’s tenure in Minnesota. Over that time frame, Wilson averaged 8.92 targets. The Minnesota coach clearly sees the value in getting a number-one receiver touches throughout the season. If New York were to trade for O’Connell, Wilson could immediately slot into the Justin Jefferson role in the Jets’ offense.
Wilson’s lack of usage in 2026 has been a glaring issue for a middling Jets offense. O'Connell acquisition seems likely to fix that. Wilson would be a day-one beneficiary if this speculation becomes reality.
Rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq would also improve with the arrival of the 41-year-old. Sadiq was drafted with high expectations and has already shown the type of game-breaking talent he possesses. The rookie has put up a 22-238-1 stat line this season, but O’Connell could take him to the next level.
The Vikings traded for T.J. Hockenson in O’Connell’s first season with the team. Since then, Hockenson has not had fewer than 50 receptions in seasons in which he has played at least 11 games. Sadiq is arguably more talented than Hockenson. With O’Connell at the helm, Jets fans would have hope that Sadiq could have seasons like Hockenson’s 2023, when he posted a 95-960-5 stat line.
Max Brosmer, Joshua Dobbs, Sam Darnold, J.J. McCarthy — these are just half the quarterbacks O’Connell has coached to a win. The coach has an offense that Kirk Cousins walked back into after three seasons away from Minnesota and threw two touchdowns to beat the Packers in Week 10. One would think that offense would follow O’Connell to New York.
Regardless of who is throwing passes for New York next season, fans would love to see O’Connell as a coach. The head coach has shown he can win and that his offense works. Even McCarthy, who many see as the coach’s biggest mistake, won his last four starts as a Viking. Whether it is Geno Smith, Cade Klubnik, a rookie, or any other option, their skills would be enhanced by O’Connell.
